## What am I solving? Please describe.
Check-in today only records attendance. There’s no way to group hackers into competing teams, reward event attendance with points, or decide prize/food pickup order from that data.

## What am I making?
A house system (4 houses per hackathon, inspired by hackUTD): each participant is in one house, earns points when checked in to events via the existing QR scan flow, and houses compete on a leaderboard. Admins use standings for prize distribution and meal pickup order. We should be able to create n amount of teams, (max 8).

Additional context
Builds on existing /admin/qr check-in and check_ins table, extend checkIn, don’t replace it
Separate from project teams (those are for submissions only)

Iteration 1: splitting people into teams randomly and adding points depending on whether they checked into an event. 
Iteration 2: will be more frontend heavy with the added designs from PD/VD teams.
title: Check-in: House system with event points, leaderboard, and prize/food pickup ordering

body:
This issue is the **framing + design-discussion doc** for adapting [guild-hall](https://github.com/cgbarlow/guild-hall) (forked here as `unsorry-guild`) into an engagement layer for the [unsorry](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry) swarm. It captures the direction that's been set and what's still open. Comment inline; decisions get folded back up into this issue.

> ### Related unsorry work — the credit model this guild rides on
> This guild's prizes and leaderboards are an engagement-layer view of unsorry's **board/credit model**, which is actively being reformed by two merged "Proposed" ADRs (both follow discussion [unsorry#3217](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry/discussions/3217) and defer provenance to ADR-023/037 — the leaderboard/provenance spec this guild already reads from):
> - **ADR-078 — sponsor-registered targets & obligation-discharge credit** ([unsorry#3232](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry/pull/3232)): moves the unit of board credit from standalone atoms to *credited obligations discharged within sponsor-registered targets* (board credit = credited obligations + targets completed, statement-hash deduped, self-target = 0; trivially-closable nodes are "glue" and earn zero; the decomposition skeleton is sponsor-authored and immutable). **This is the closest unsorry concept to our "prize":** a guild prize is effectively the engagement-layer face of a sponsor-registered target, and per-prize ranking should count ADR-078 credited obligations rather than raw atom/proof counts.
> - **ADR-079 — deterministic solver provider** ([unsorry#3246](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry/pull/3246)): adds an optional sympy provider with a **board-submission guard** — deterministically-farmable easy goals can't earn board credit without a credit-reform attestation. The guild's leaderboards/prizes must **honor the same guard** so a proof-factory can't top a prize board.
> **Net:** the score basis in Decision #3 (`difficulty_points×100 + proofs×25`, ADR-023) is the *current* board formula and is itself being reformed — the guild should track the **ADR-023 → ADR-078 → ADR-079** credit chain rather than hard-code today's formula. See **Decision #3** and **Open items** below.

## Why we're doing this

unsorry is a swarm that proves theorems. We want to **encourage contributors in the swarm to work toward specified goals**, and the lever is engagement: present goals as **prizes / badges**, run **leaderboards** per goal, and award **badges** that live on contributor profiles. guild-hall already is a "quest → badge → leaderboard → profile" engine, so we fork it and bend it to point at unsorry's goals instead of generic quests. Secondarily, `unsorry-guild` becomes the new home for unsorry's existing public pages (leaderboard, showcase, proof graph, queue).

## What each side gives us (grounding)

**guild-hall today** (Next.js 15 App Router + Supabase + Netlify, TanStack Query, shadcn/ui):
- A full **quest → objective → points → achievement/badge → tier → leaderboard → profile** model in Supabase (~24 tables, 140+ migrations). Achievements already support criteria types `quest_count` / `points_total` / `streak` / `manual` (`supabase/migrations/010_achievements.sql`).
- A **privacy-respecting leaderboard** computed as a Postgres view (`supabase/migrations/060_view_leaderboard.sql`).
- **Auth** via Supabase (email/password + Google/Apple OAuth), roles `admin` / `gm` / `member`, middleware-protected routes (`src/middleware.ts`, `src/lib/auth/`), plus a lot of email/onboarding/digest surface.
- A **categories** table + per-quest filter dropdown (`supabase/migrations/004_*`, `src/components/quests/quest-filters.tsx`) — the closest existing thing to a "domain" filter, but it's per-quest, not a site-wide context.
- Theming: `light` / `warm` / `dark`; default is currently `warm` (`src/app/layout.tsx`). Dark already exists as a full theme.

**unsorry today** (the data we'd point at):
- **Identity = GitHub username.** Contributors are credited via `solver≜<handle>` provenance records in `library/index/*.aisp` (ADR-023). No emails, no accounts, no real names.
- **The repo is the database.** Goals (`goals/*.aisp`), proofs (`library/Unsorry/*.lean`), proof metadata (`library/index/*.aisp`), run facts (`proof-runs/*.aisp`) and commit history are the single source of truth.
- The **four pages** (`docs/leaderboard.html`, `docs/showcase.html`, `docs/proofs-contributors-visualisation.html` + `proof-graph.svg`, `docs/queue.html`) are static HTML+Tailwind+vanilla-JS, **generated by GitHub Actions** (`tools/leaderboard`, `tools/visualiser`, `tools/queue_board`) into JSON artifacts (`docs/metrics/*.json`) and served from **GitHub Pages**. Queue is live from `queued/prove/*` branches + the GitHub PR API.
- **No formal goals/prizes system** — just a worklist (`docs/targets.md`) and a difficulty-weighted leaderboard (`score = difficulty_points*100 + verified_proofs*25`, ADR-023).
- **ADR-030** (the domain-agnostic workload engine, roadmap Phase 6, **not yet started**): a "domain" is a plugin implementing `generate/verify/decompose/assimilate`, with verifiability tiers `VERIFIED` / `SCORED` / `CONSENSUS`. **Math = Lean = VERIFIED**, and is the only domain that exists.

## Decisions

1. **Auth & identity → admin-only, GitHub everywhere else.** Strip the email/password + OAuth login, registration, onboarding, and email/digest machinery; the only authenticated role is **admin** (Supabase auth). Everyone else is anonymous, public, read-only. Contributors are **GitHub handles**, auto-sourced from unsorry's git provenance (no signup); profiles are keyed on the handle (e.g. `/u/<handle>`). guild-hall's quest lifecycle (accept → submit-evidence → GM-review) is **removed** — completion is git-verified. **Admin scope:** define prizes & criteria, run seasons (open/close + confirm the podium), grant manual/discretionary badges, and curate content (showcase, banners, featured proofs). _(Blast radius: `src/lib/auth/`, `src/middleware.ts`, email-preference tables, RLS policies, `user_quests`/`user_objectives`/evidence/GM-review.)_

2. **Data architecture → slim Supabase overlay over git.** **git is the source of truth**: all proof / contributor / leaderboard data is read from unsorry's git artifacts. A **slim Supabase overlay** holds only the guild-specific concepts that don't exist in unsorry's git — prize definitions, completion criteria, awards/podium results, and admin-curated content. Computed standings & badge-eligibility are **recomputed from the git artifacts on read (short cache)**, not persisted; the overlay stores only authored config plus **frozen closed-season results**.

3. **Prizes = flagship targets, difficulty-weighted & seasoned.** A prize is a **flagship target** — a headline goal (`goal id`) plus its dependency / sub-lemma tree — and there can be **multiple** flagship targets running at once. Clicking a prize opens its **own per-prize leaderboard**, ranking contributors by **difficulty-weighted discharge** (`difficulty_points×100 + credited_proofs×25`, ADR-023, tracking the ADR-023 → 078 → 079 chain) of that target's tree. The **season closes when the target's headline goal is proved**; the admin then **confirms the podium** (**1st / 2nd / 3rd**), with **"contributor"** for anyone with ≥1 proof in the tree. Each prize shows a **live progress indicator** toward completion (% of the target's tree discharged + a target-scoped proof-graph/dependency view, reusing unsorry's proof-graph data). Badges land on the contributor's **profile** (reusing guild-hall's badge/profile UI). **Attribution plumbing:** `swarm/run.sh` and `swarm/agent.sh` already accept `--goal <id>`; extend this to **target-awareness** (a `--target <id>` spanning the target's goal set) across `swarm/run.sh` / `agent.sh` / `sourcing.sh` so a contributor can flag from the CLI which flagship target they're working toward — that flag is what attributes runs to a prize. _(unsorry-side change; PR held.)_

4. **Domain context → URL-prefixed, new top axis.** A site-wide header **domain selector** implemented as a **URL prefix** (`/math/...`), a **new top-level axis above** guild-hall's categories (categories become sub-filters within a domain). It filters leaderboard, showcase, proof graph, queue, prizes, and profiles. Ship the dropdown now with **Math as the only option**; per-tier (`SCORED`/`CONSENSUS`) UI is deferred until a second domain exists. This is the UI seam for ADR-030. The **domain registry is a PR-reviewed file in the unsorry repo** (git, ADR-030-aligned), read by the guild like any other artifact; unsorry's **generators stamp a `domain` field** on each record (constant `math` today) so the ported pages can filter. _(unsorry-side; PRs held.)_

5. **The four pages → reimplement as Next pages.** Rebuild **leaderboard, showcase, proof graph, queue** as React/Next pages, inheriting the header, domain selector, dark theme, and nav rather than being bolted on. **Sourcing per surface (refined per [maintainer note](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry-guild/issues/1#issuecomment-4760688846)):**
   - **Leaderboard + profiles' global standing are Decision-#2 surfaces — recompute from the raw git records on read** (`library/index/*.aisp`, `goals/*.aisp`/`goal_effort`, `proof-runs/*.aisp`), which the proof-merge PRs commit in real time. This structurally removes any GitHub-Actions/cron lag in the derived `leaderboard-ui.json`. The baked `leaderboard-ui.json` is only a **stopgap** (now near-real-time again via unsorry#3735, push-on-merge + cron backstop). *(Per-target leaderboards already recompute from `library/index` — consistent.)*
   - **Showcase / proof graph / queue** consume the generated artifacts (`showcase.html`, `proof-graph.svg`, `docs/queue.json`) — generators stay in unsorry.
   - **Timeline caveat:** the proofs-over-time series (`timelines.merge` / `timelines.solve`, cumulative hourly buckets from commit history) is too heavy to recompute per request — keep a periodically-built cache for that series even in the recompute-on-read model (see Open items).

6. **Theme → dark default, keep the toggle.** Dark is the default (`src/app/layout.tsx` → `defaultTheme="dark"`); the `light` / `warm` options stay.

7. **Repo strategy → hard fork, prune later.** Fully diverge from guild-hall. Disable dead surface (auth/email/quest-lifecycle) behind flags now to ship fast; **aggressive prune + migration squash after the first vertical slice validates the model** (see Suggested first slice). We won't track upstream guild-hall.

8. **Hosting → guild on its own subdomain.** Deploy `unsorry-guild` to **Netlify at `swarm.unsorry.agentics.org.nz`**; unsorry's existing pages stay at `unsorry.agentics.org.nz`. The two sites **coexist** — no DNS cutover or Pages retirement now (revisit later if desired). unsorry's generators keep emitting the JSON artifacts the guild reads either way.

## Open items

Design direction is settled. What remains is implementation detail (for the plan stage) and cross-repo work in unsorry (PRs **held** until the plan is approved — see the PR-hold note).

**Deferred to the plan stage (implementation detail):**
- Overlay table schema (`prizes`, `criteria`, `targets`, `awards`/frozen-season-results, admin content) and the recompute-on-read **cache TTL**.
- Exact derivation of a target's **dependency / sub-lemma tree** from `goals/*.aisp` `deps` (what counts toward a prize, and toward the progress indicator).
- Per-tier (`SCORED` / `CONSENSUS`) UI — deferred until a second domain exists.
- **Recompute-on-read leaderboard fidelity** (Decision #5): the live recompute must faithfully reproduce the official score components — `dispatch_points`, contributor-alias merging (`contributor-aliases.json`), and inferred-git-author proofs — or it diverges from unsorry's board. Until that's ported, the baked `leaderboard-ui.json` (fresh via unsorry#3735) remains the source; the recompute path is the structural target.
- **Timeline-series cache** (Decision #5 caveat): keep a periodically-built cache for `timelines.merge`/`timelines.solve` rather than scanning commit history on each request.

**Cross-repo work in unsorry (PRs on hold):**
1. **Target-awareness in the swarm CLI** — extend the existing `--goal <id>` (in `swarm/run.sh`, `agent.sh`) to a `--target <id>` across `run.sh` / `agent.sh` / `sourcing.sh`, so runs attribute to a flagship target. *(drives Decision #3)*
2. **Domain registry file** (git, PR-reviewed) in unsorry. *(Decision #4)*
3. **Stamp a `domain` field** on the generated artifacts (`leaderboard` / `visualiser` / `queue_board`). *(Decision #4)*
4. *(future)* Promote the **ADR-035 triviality battery from advisory to a blocking gate** (the "blocking triviality gate").
5. *(future)* A **goal / target issue template** extending `propose-goal.md` / `propose-target.md`.
6. *(future)* The **ADR-078 `targets/` registry** as the eventual backing for prizes (today: `goals/*.aisp` + difficulty).

## Suggested first slice

A thin vertical to de-risk the model before the big build:
1. **Theme + auth (#6, #1)** — dark default; rip out login/registration/email; reduce to public read-only + a single admin.
2. **Read-only leaderboard + profiles** sourced from unsorry's existing `docs/metrics/leaderboard-ui.json`, keyed on GitHub handle (proves the git-as-source path).
3. **One hardcoded "Math" domain** wired as a URL-prefixed header context that filters that leaderboard (proves the ADR-030 seam).
4. **One flagship-target prize** end-to-end — a target (goal id + dependency tree), its per-prize seasoned leaderboard, a live progress indicator, and podium + contributor badges on profiles (proves the novel mechanic).

## Appendix — unsorry integration reference (facts the build depends on)

Concrete unsorry-side facts the `unsorry-guild` build relies on, captured here so this issue is self-contained.

### A. Data artifacts the guild reads (git-native, generated by unsorry CI)
All live under unsorry's `docs/`, regenerated by GitHub Actions and committed to `main`:

| Artifact | Generator / workflow | Cadence | Feeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `docs/metrics/leaderboard-ui.json` (+ `community-stats.json`, `attribution-gaps.json`, `sourcing-leaderboard.json`) | `tools/leaderboard` / `leaderboard.yml` | **on merge (push); cron backstop** (unsorry#3735 — previously cron-only `*/10`, throttled to ~1/h) | Leaderboard + profiles (stopgap — see Decision #5) |
| `docs/proof-graph.svg`, `docs/proofs-contributors-visualisation.html` | `tools/visualiser` / `proofs-visualisation.yml` | on push to `main` | Proof graph |
| `docs/queue.html`, `docs/queue.json` | `tools/queue_board` / `queue-board.yml` | ~15 min | Queue |
| `docs/showcase.html` | hand-authored | manual | Showcase |

Leaderboard contributor record shape (`leaderboard-ui.json`):
```
{ github, display_name ("@handle"), avatar_url, rank, score,
  difficulty_points, credited_proofs, attempt_yield,
  badges: { difficulty, proofs, success_rate_percent },
  credit_sources: ["explicit-solver", "inferred-git-add-author"] }
```
The **board score is precomputed** in the artifact: `score = difficulty_points*100 + credited_proofs*25` (rank 1 today: 1688×100 + 811×25 = 189,075). The guild can consume `score`/`rank` directly, or recompute per-prize from the same fields. **Identity key = `github` handle** (matches Decision #1). This file is the natural source for the first-slice leaderboard + profiles.

### B. Hosting today (relevant to the Decision #5 cutover)
- unsorry Pages: **legacy Jekyll**, served from **`main:/`** (docs/ served at the site root), custom domain **`unsorry.agentics.org.nz`**, HTTPS enforced. **No Pages deploy workflow** — Pages auto-rebuilds whenever a generator commits to `main`.
- Generators push straight to `main` with a `REFRESH_TOKEN` admin PAT + `[skip ci]`, bypassing branch protection.
- Retiring/redirecting = stop the doc-commits and repoint the CNAME / add redirects; there is no workflow to disable.

### C. Goal authoring today (relevant to Decision #3 prize-criterion vocabulary)
- Issue templates already exist: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/propose-goal.md` and `propose-target.md` (classic markdown + frontmatter; sections: summary, skeleton, "already established", non-triviality, absence from mathlib, difficulty/scope). A guild "goal/prize template" should **extend these, not reinvent them**.
- A goal is an AISP record (`Skills/unsorry-goal-sourcing/assets/goal-record.aisp.tmpl`): fields `id, phase, status (open/proved/archived), difficulty (1–5), src (backlog/*.md), deps, lean (goals/*.lean), sha, aff (affinity)`, plus a Lean statement file.
- unsorry's swarm CLI already supports targeting: `swarm/run.sh` and `swarm/agent.sh` accept `--goal <id>` (restrict/override selection to one goal); `swarm/sourcing.sh` is theme/pool-driven (no `--goal`). The flagship-target plumbing (Decision #3) extends this to a `--target <id>` across all three.
- **ADR-078's `targets/` registry does not exist yet** — sponsor-registered targets are *proposed only*. So "model a prize on an ADR-078 target" is forward-looking; **today a prize must be defined against `goals/*.aisp` + difficulty**.

### D. Credit & anti-farm mechanics (the substrate under Decision #3)
- **Board score basis** = ADR-023 (`difficulty_points` + `credited_proofs`), being reformed by ADR-078 (credited obligations) — see the top callout.
- **ADR-035 triviality battery** (Status: **Accepted**): tactics `rfl | trivial | decide | norm_num | omega | simp | simp_all | aesop | ring | linarith | tauto`; deliberately **excludes** `nlinarith | positivity | field_simp | gcongr` (reserved for ADR-078 registration probes). Tool: `tools/sourcing/check_triviality.py`.
- It is **advisory at merge today**: `.github/workflows/triviality.yml` posts a sticky comment and **always exits 0** — explicitly *not* a required check; the real block is **at sourcing admission (a human step)**. The "blocking triviality gate" idea is *promoting this to a blocking gate* (future, on hold).
- **Required status checks on `main`** (branch protection): **`gate-a`** (soundness — kernel re-verify, axiom audit, statement binding) and **`gate-b`**. Triviality is *not* among them.
- **ADR-078 and ADR-079 are both Status: Proposed (2026-06-20)**; their SPEC files aren't in the tree yet. The credit reform is *direction*, not yet shipped.

---

_Adapting [cgbarlow/guild-hall](https://github.com/cgbarlow/guild-hall) → `agenticsnz/unsorry-guild`. Related unsorry work: ADR-030 (domain-agnostic workload engine, Phase 6), ADR-023 (proof provenance & leaderboard), ADR-078 / [#3232](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry/pull/3232) (sponsor-registered targets & obligation-discharge credit), ADR-079 / [#3246](https://github.com/agenticsnz/unsorry/pull/3246) (deterministic solver provider & board-submission guard)._

body:
## The Risk

Apple's App Store guideline 4.2 (Minimum Functionality) requires that an app include features that "elevate it beyond a repackaged website" and is "not primarily... a collection of links." Apple reviewers specifically reject multi-game apps that feel like a container rather than a product — one where the games could just as easily have been separate apps or a website.

**BC Arcade currently has:**
- 12 games (6 free, 6 premium via entitlement JWT)
- Per-game leaderboards (most without even a dedicated UI screen)
- A profile showing total games, favorite game, top score, games tried
- No cross-game XP, currency, levels, or achievements
- No daily challenge system spanning multiple games
- Session-anonymous (no account/sign-in)

Profiles and leaderboards alone are not sufficient. Research across approved multi-game apps (Microsoft Solitaire Collection, GAMEE Prizes, Daily Pastimes) shows Apple reviewers look for **functional evidence** that the collection is one product — specifically: a shared economy, a daily hook that opens the *app* rather than a specific game, and at least one feature that couldn't exist on a website.

---

## What Approved Multi-Game Apps All Have

| Feature | Microsoft Solitaire | GAMEE Prizes | Daily Pastimes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shared currency/points | ✅ unified coins + XP | ✅ tickets | ✅ diamond ranking |
| Daily cross-game challenge | ✅ spans all 5 variants | ✅ tournaments | ✅ timed daily rounds |
| Unified leaderboard | ✅ Game Center | ✅ global | ✅ cross-game |
| Seasonal events | ✅ platform-wide | ✅ prize draws | — |
| Native OS integration | ✅ Game Center, Xbox | ✅ Game Center | ✅ Game Center |

---

## Recommended Approach for BC Arcade

These are ordered by impact-to-effort and tailored to what the codebase already has.

### Tier 1 — Minimum viable (do before submission)

**1. Arcade XP and player level**
The backend already aggregates `total_games`, `best`, and `avg` per game in `/stats/me`. A lightweight XP formula (e.g. base XP per game completed + bonus for score percentile) can be computed server-side and surfaced as a player level on the profile screen. This reuses existing data with no new game-side changes.

**2. Daily cross-game challenge**
A single daily mission that requires playing 2–3 different games (e.g. "Complete a Solitaire game and reach wave 3 in StarSwarm"). The Daily Word game already has the server-side daily puzzle infrastructure; the challenge system can reuse that pattern. This is the single highest-signal feature — it proves the app is one product, and it gives players a reason to open BC Arcade (not Blackjack, not Solitaire — *BC Arcade*) every day.

**3. Visible progression on the home screen**
The lobby should show the player's current XP level and daily challenge status prominently. Players should see their progress before choosing a game, not after.

**4. Game Center integration**
One shared Game Center leaderboard per game (all under the same app identity) plus a cross-game "Total Games Played" achievement. This is native iOS infrastructure that a website cannot replicate — it directly addresses the 4.2 concern.

**5. Notes for Review**
Before submission, write explicit review notes describing the shared systems: "Play any game to earn XP toward your player level. Today's daily challenge requires completing a Solitaire hand and a StarSwarm run. All progress persists under one profile." Reviewers spend ~5 minutes with an app; tell them exactly where to look.

---

### Tier 2 — Strong differentiators (do soon after launch)

**6. Cross-game unlock system**
Blackjack already has a working unlock system (`frontend/src/game/blackjack/unlocks.ts`) with three reward types (table_theme, card_back, chip_style). The natural next step is expanding this into a platform-wide achievement and cosmetic system — milestones in any game unlock cosmetics that apply across relevant games. This also resolves the open design question in issue #1911.

**7. Platform-wide seasonal events**
A lobby-level campaign (holiday theme, special challenge week) that applies visual theming and bonus XP across all games simultaneously. This creates the visual cohesion that signals "product" to both reviewers and players.

**8. Single premium subscription**
The entitlement JWT already gates 6 games. Reframing this as a single "BC Arcade Premium" subscription (rather than per-game unlocks) strengthens the "one product" narrative in the App Store listing and in the reviewer's experience.

---

### Tier 3 — Gold standard (backlog)

- Tiered loyalty status (Bronze → Gold → Platinum) based on Arcade XP, with visible benefits
- Cross-game challenges that unlock content in a different game than the one you played
- In-App Events published to Apple's Games app for seasonal campaigns (WWDC25 Session 215)
- Social layer via Game Center Challenges for cross-player competition

---

## Suggested Priority Order

1. Arcade XP + player level (reuses existing `/stats/me` data — low backend cost)
2. Daily cross-game challenge (highest reviewer impact; Daily Word infrastructure already exists)
3. Home screen progression display
4. Game Center leaderboard integration
5. Platform cosmetics / expand unlock system (resolves #1911)
6. Premium subscription reframing

---

### Project Name

AI Debate Casino

### Team Members

Keith Wegner

### Summary

**AI Debate Casino** is a multiplayer fake-chip debate game where a host creates a room, players join, vote on topics, place bets, buy heckle cards, chat, and react as an audience jury. AI generates debate topics, personas, betting markets, debate turns, and a structured judge verdict that settles the round and updates the leaderboard. The app uses a lightweight Node server, static browser UI, Server-Sent Events for live updates, and optional Redis/Valkey persistence for hosted rooms. It can run locally with real OpenAI API calls or in mock mode for no-token testing. The project was also developed with AI assistance for implementation, debugging, UI iteration, regression tests, and GitHub workflow support.

### Primary Link

https://github.com/keithwegner/ai-debate-casino

### Live Demo

https://ai-debate-casino.onrender.com/

### Demo Video

_No response_

### Drive Folder

_No response_

### Quick Start / Review Instructions

## Live Demo

[Start an AI debate game](https://ai-debate-casino.onrender.com/)

Login code is `KeithsCasino`.

## Local Testing / Experimentation

Clone repository:

```sh
git clone <repo-url>
cd ai-debate-casino
cp .env.example .env
npm install
npm run check
npm start
```

Open: 

```sh
http://localhost:8787
```

For local testing without OpenAI token usage:

```sh
npm run mock
```

Recommended demo flow:

1. Host creates a room.
2. Players join with the room code/link.
3. Players suggest/vote on topics.
4. Host assigns debaters and posts odds.
5. Players place fake-chip bets, chat, heckle, and react.
6. Host starts the debate.
7. AI judge scores the round and settles the leaderboard.

### AI Tools Used

- OpenAI API for runtime AI generation and judging.
- Codex / AI coding assistant for development support, implementation, debugging, testing, and UI iteration.
- Mock AI mode for deterministic local testing without API calls.

### How AI Was Used

In the app:

- Generate debate topic candidates.
- Normalize custom topics.
- Generate custom debater personas.
- Create betting markets and odds.
- Generate AI debater turns.
- Judge completed debates with structured scoring.
- Compare judge results against audience jury reactions.

In development:

- Assisted with feature implementation and refactoring.
- Helped design and debug mobile UX fixes.
- Generated and refined tests for render and smoke coverage.
- Supported visual redesign work and accessibility/readability improvements.
- Helped manage GitHub issue/PR workflows.

### Known Constraints

- Fake chips only; no real-money betting, prizes, or cash value.
- Local state is in-memory unless Redis/Valkey is configured.
- Active debate generation does not resume across server restarts.
- Host identity is stored in browser local storage, not full authentication.
- Invite-code access is a simple shared gate, not role-based auth.
- AI moderation is lightweight and not production-grade trust/safety.
- OpenAI-backed runs depend on API key availability, latency, and token cost.

### Optional Notes

The app is designed as a hackathon-friendly multiplayer AI game. It prioritizes fast setup, live room interaction, spectator participation, and replayability over production auth or real-money mechanics. It can be run fully in mock mode for demos, or with an OpenAI API key for generated topics, debaters, odds, debate turns, and judging.

> **Part of the Community Manual Library epic — Gerromie/maintenance-crew#515.** Site-repo work.

## Contributor recognition & gamification

### What

Recognize the people who contribute manuals to the library — "street cred" for engaged community members who help others. Driven entirely off the **optional attribution** captured at submission (intake issue) and the merged-manual history:

- A generated **contributors page / section** in the repo (and/or on `maintenancecrew.app`) that calls out contributors by their chosen display name / handle.
- **Submission counts** per contributor and a **leaderboard / rank** by contributions.
- **Badges / tiers** for milestones (first manual, 5, 10, 25, …; rare-equipment finds; etc.) — recognition people actually enjoy.
- Regenerated automatically whenever submissions are merged (same Action cadence as the discovery index).

### Why

People love recognition. Counts, ranks, and badges turn a one-time good deed into ongoing engagement, which is exactly what grows a community-sourced library. It costs us almost nothing (it's derived from data we already capture) and meaningfully increases the odds that someone publishes their parse instead of keeping it.

### Who benefits

- **Engaged contributors** — visible credit and status for helping others.
- **The library** — gamification is a growth flywheel for content.
- **New users** — a visible, active contributor community is a trust signal.

### Proposed approach

- Derive recognition data from merged-manual metadata (display name / handle + counts), keyed off the optional identity stored by the intake broker. **Respect anonymity** — anonymous submissions count toward the library but carry no public attribution.
- A GitHub Action regenerates a contributors manifest + a human-facing page/section (e.g. `CONTRIBUTORS.md` and/or a Pages section) on each publish.
- Define badge/tier rules (submission-count milestones to start; room for more later).
- Optionally expose a contributor/badge feed the **app** can surface (e.g. show a contributor's badge, or "you've contributed N manuals") — app-side display can be a follow-up; the data contract lives here.

### Non-goals

- Collecting any PII beyond the small, optional, user-chosen attribution fields (intake issue).
- Real-money rewards / leaderboards with prizes.
- Exposing contributors who chose to stay anonymous.
- The in-app badge UI itself (possible follow-up; this issue produces the data + repo-side recognition).

### Additional context

- **Epic:** maintenance-crew#515. **Depends on:** the intake issue (optional identity capture) and the storage model. **Pairs with:** the discovery-index generation Action (same regenerate-on-merge pattern).
- Privacy posture inherited from the epic: minimal-PII, consent-gated, anonymous-by-default with opt-in attribution.

- Sections: Prize (cards), Rules (clear bullets + judging criteria), final CTA anchored to a registration form or external form.
- Smooth scroll for anchors, subtle micro-interactions (hover, entrance fades).
- Fully responsive: mobile, tablet, desktop.
- Accessibility: semantic HTML, keyboard navigable, ARIA where needed, contrast accessible where possible.
- Performance target: initial load under 1.5s on 3G simulated; Lighthouse performance/accessibility >= 90.
- Analytics: basic event tracking for CTA clicks and form submissions.

Target audience
- Developers, ML researchers, makers building agent-based systems (single- or multi-agent).
- Comfortable with Git/GitHub; expect repo + demo/video submission.

Design direction (Wes Anderson inspiration)
- Composition: strict vertical symmetry in the hero with decorative horizontal bands and centered hero card.
- Palette (example):
  - Custard Yellow: #F6E7B4
  - Salmon Pink: #F7A99A
  - Muted Teal: #7FB3B3
  - Oxford Indigo: #2E4057
  - Cream/Beige: #E8D5C4
- Typography:
  - Headings: Playful geometric sans (closest: Montserrat or Poppins; if available use Futura/Brandon Grotesque).
  - Subhead/body: Serif for contrast (Playfair Display or Merriweather).
  - Use Google Fonts: Montserrat (700/500) + Playfair Display (400/700).
- Imagery/illustration:
  - Custom illustration: symmetrical scene with agent(s) in a stylized, retro-robot/character lineup, centered, with simple props; flat colors, thick outlines.
  - Decorative horizontal stripes or frames on top and bottom of hero.
  - Provide SVG patterns and icons (prize trophy, rule checklist, clock).
- Layout details:
  - Hero height: 70vh desktop, 45vh mobile.
  - Container max-width: 1100px, center aligned.
  - Generous whitespace, narrow text columns for rules.

Content (copy suggestions)
- Hero:
  - Headline: “Agent Building Hackathon”
  - Subhead: “Design. Train. Deploy. Compete — Build intelligent agents that solve real problems.”
  - Date/format line: “Submission deadline: May 21, 2026 • Remote • Teams up to 4”
  - Primary CTA in hero: “Register Now” (anchors to #register)
  - Secondary microcopy under CTA: “Prizes. Mentors. Live demos.”
- Prize section:
  - Headline: “Prizes & Perks”
  - Top prize card examples:
    - 1st Place — $5,000 + mentorship + feature in showcase
    - 2nd Place — $2,000 + mentorship
    - Runner Ups — $500 swag + platform credits
  - Additional perks: access to mentors, cloud credits, job matchmaking, winner interview.
- Rules section:
  - Headline: “Rules & Submission”
  - Bullets:
    - Team size: up to 4 people.
    - Submission: GitHub repo + README + 3-minute demo video hosted on YouTube or Vimeo.
    - License: open-source preferred (MIT/Apache recommended).
    - Allowed resources: open-source libraries, public APIs; no proprietary datasets without rights.
    - Judges: panel of 5 (names optional).
    - Judging criteria (weights): Innovation 30%, Technical implementation 30%, Impact 20%, Presentation 20%.
    - Timeline: registration open date, submission deadline, judging window, winners announced.
    - Code of Conduct summary + link to full doc.
- Final CTA (register):
  - Headline: “Ready to build?”
  - Button: “Register / Submit” (primary)
  - Secondary option: “Join Slack” or “Read the full rules”
  - Microcopy: “Need help? Email support@yourorg.example”

Component specs & interactions

Header
- Sticky top bar with logo (left) + anchor links (Prize, Rules, Register).
- On small screens, hamburger menu that reveals anchor list in a slide-down panel.
- Anchor link behavior: smooth-scroll, update URL hash without page reload, active link highlight on scroll.
- Accessibility: “Skip to content” link at top.

Hero banner
- Visual: centered illustrated panel (SVG) surrounded by decorative frames/stripes.
- Typography scale: H1 ~ clamp(28px, 5vw, 56px); Subhead ~ clamp(16px, 2.4vw, 22px).
- CTA layout: primary CTA (strong color), secondary text link below.
- Animations:
  - Entrance: gentle fade + small upward translate for hero copy (duration 600ms, easing cubic-bezier).
  - Background motif: slight parallax on scroll (subtle, not heavy).
  - Hover states: CTA lift (translateY(-4px)), shadow increase.

Prize cards
- Grid layout: 1 column mobile, 2 columns tablet, 3 columns desktop.
- Each card: icon (SVG trophy/medal), title, short copy, badge for cash amount.
- Interaction: hover elevates card + subtle border color reveal (Teal or Indigo).
- Accessibility: text-based details not only in visuals.

Rules block
- Two-column layout on desktop: rules left, judging criteria right (or stacked on mobile).
- Use numbered lists for rules, with clear headings (Eligibility, Submission, Judging, Timeline).
- Provide downloadable PDF link for full rules.

Registration CTA & Form
- Option A: Inline form anchored at bottom (#register)
  - Fields: Team name (optional), Primary contact (name + email), GitHub org/user, Short project idea (optional), Consent checkbox (rules & code of conduct), Submit button.
  - Client validation + server-side validation. On success, show confirmation message and link to submission instructions.
  - Accessible: label elements, aria-invalid on error, focus set to success message.
  - Example flow: Register → confirmation with next steps + Slack invite link emailed.
- Option B (preferred if you already use Google Forms/Typeform): CTA opens external form in new tab or a modal with iframe. If iframe used, ensure focus trap and accessible titles.
- CTA styling: wide pill-shaped button (border-radius 999px), 48px height on desktop, full-width on mobile.

Button design (primary CTA)
- Default: background-color: #2E4057 (indigo), color: #E8D5C4 (cream). Or solid custard with navy text as alternate.
- Hover: lighten background or add subtle shadow; transform: translateY(-3px).
- Focus: visible outline (2px contrast color), accessible focus ring.
- Disabled: low opacity, aria-disabled attribute.
- Icon in button (optional): small right chevron or ticket icon; ensure sufficient hit area.

Accessibility & SEO
- Semantic HTML: header, main, section, nav, footer.
- ARIA: aria-current for active nav, aria-labels for form inputs and modal, role="dialog" for modal.
- Color contrast checks for text on background—if hero uses muted pastel backgrounds with large headings, ensure heading contrast meets AA (4.5:1 for normal text; headings can be larger but still aim for at least 3:1).
- Meta tags: title, description, Open Graph (og:title, og:description, og:image), twitter card.
- Structured data: Event schema (Event) / Organization if applicable.
- Robots: index, follow.

Assets to produce
- Hero SVG illustration: center-focused, 3 variants (desktop wide, tablet, mobile crop); layered SVG with separate decorative elements for parallax animation.
- Logo SVG & favicon.
- Icons (SVG): trophy, medal, rules/checklist, clock/calendar, mentor/person.
- PDF of full rules.
- Fonts via Google Fonts: Montserrat & Playfair Display (link rel preconnect + preload for font-display:swap).

CSS tokens (examples)
- --color-primary: #2E4057
- --color-accent-1: #F6E7B4
- --color-accent-2: #F7A99A
- --color-accent-3: #7FB3B3
- --bg: #E8D5C4
- --text: #2E4057
- --radius-pill: 999px
- Spacing: 8px baseline (4,8,16,24,32,48,...)
- Breakpoints: mobile: 0–599px, tablet: 600–1023px, desktop: 1024px+

HTML structure (skeleton)
- header.nav
  - .logo, nav links (a[href="#prize"], a[href="#rules"], a[href="#register"])
- main
  - section#hero
    - .hero-inner (title, subtitle, date, CTA)
    - svg.hero-illustration
  - section#prize
    - grid of prize cards
  - section#rules
    - rules content + judging criteria
  - section#register
    - registration card or link to external form + FAQ microcopy
- footer
  - contact, social, Code of Conduct link, legal

JS behavior
- Smooth scroll on anchor clicks (history.pushState or scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'})).
- Set active nav based on scroll position (IntersectionObserver).
- Modal handling for registration (if used): trap focus, close on ESC, return focus to trigger.
- Form validation and submit handler (POST to event API). Show success/failure UI states.
- Event tracking hooks: CTA clicks, form submission events, video play events.

Performance & build considerations
- Use optimized SVGs; inlined critical hero SVG where appropriate to reduce requests.
- Lazy-load non-critical images (loading="lazy").
- Minify CSS + JS; critical CSS inlined for above-the-fold hero.
- Use HTTP caching and compression.
- Preconnect to Google Fonts, preload key fonts.

Acceptance criteria (developer QA checklist)
- All anchor nav links smoothly scroll to correct sections and URL hash updates.
- Hero matches supplied design token palette and font styling; illustrations available and scale correctly.
- Prize grid and rules content match provided copy and adapt responsively (1/2/3 columns).
- CTA opens registration (modal or external) and form is keyboard accessible and validates inputs.
- Colors meet accessibility contrast guidelines for body text and interactive elements.
- Page loads under target performance budget and passes Lighthouse audits (performance, accessibility >= 90).
- Analytics events fire for CTA and form submission.
- Cross-browser on Chrome, Firefox, Safari (mobile & desktop).

Deliverables for hand-off
- Figma/Sketch mockups for desktop, tablet, mobile (hero + prize + rules + register).
- SVG/PNG assets listed above, optimized.
- Font license links and CSS import snippets.
- Copy as final text (provided above, editable).
- API endpoints for form submission (or URL for external form).
- Accessibility checklist & test cases.

Estimated timeline (guideline)
- Design: 2–3 days (hero illustration + responsive mocks).
- Front-end development: 3–5 days (responsive layout, animations, form integration).
- QA & accessibility testing: 1–2 days.
- Total: 6–10 working days.

Example microcopy & button states
- Primary button default: “Register Now”
- Hover: “Register Now →”
- Submitted: “Registration received” (show a green check icon)
- Error: “Submission failed — try again” (explain next steps)

Optional enhancements (phase 2)
- Live leaderboard for submissions.
- Embedded demo player or live streams.
- User accounts and submission dashboard.
- Multi-language support.

If you’d like, I can:
- produce a ready-to-implement CSS variables file + a minimal HTML/CSS/JS starter template for devs, or
- create Figma-style layout specs and responsive measurements for the hero and prize grid.

Which would you prefer next: starter code (HTML/CSS/JS) or design mockups (Figma specs)?

## Summary

Ingest the [Kaggle Morse Learning Machine Challenge v2](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/morse-learning-machine-challenge-v2) dataset as a **third external benchmark** alongside `training-set-a` (real OTA) and the adversarial synthetic suite (PR #417). Use it to (a) get a defensible external metric for our decoder, (b) cross-validate the `augment-arrl` (PR TBD) augmentation distributions, and (c) stress-test wider WPM range than our current suites cover.

## Dataset facts

- 200 WAV files, mono, 32-bit float, 8 kHz
- ~100 labeled (training, in `SampleSubmission.csv`); ~100 unlabeled (validation, scored via submission)
- Per-file randomization:
  - SNR: -14 to +20 dB
  - Pitch: 600 - 1200 Hz
  - Speed: 12 - 80 WPM
- Filename convention: `cw001.wav` ... `cw200.wav`
- Scoring metric: Levenshtein distance (== our CER, conveniently)

Reference baseline solution: https://github.com/talengu/kaggle_morse

## Why it matters

1. **External metric.** We have been grading our own homework on a 6-sample real OTA bench (training-set-a). The Kaggle leaderboard gives us a public, third-party number — useful for sanity checking and as a defensible "v1 done" signal.
2. **Augmentation distribution validation.** The competition's `(SNR ∈ [-14,+20], WPM ∈ [12,80], pitch ∈ [600,1200])` is exactly what `augment-arrl` is synthesizing. If our augmented corpus does not bracket the Kaggle distribution, our augmenter is mis-tuned. Cheap to check via histogram overlay.
3. **WPM stress test.** Our current bench tops out at 40 WPM. The Kaggle 50-80 WPM tail is something we never exercise. The two-pass WPM seed (PR #423) needs to be re-validated at high WPM since the bias-correction constants were tuned at 13-40 WPM.
4. **Independent overfitting check.** If we only optimize for training-set-a + adversarial-suite, we will silently overfit those distributions. Kaggle is held-out by construction.

## What this is NOT

- Not a training corpus. ~100 labeled files is too small for neural training. Our augmented ARRL corpus (~535 h, ~47k variants from `augment-arrl`) dwarfs it by 3+ orders of magnitude.
- Not "real world" — synthetic CW + AWGN, no Watterson channel, no QRM, no human fist variability. Beating Kaggle is necessary but not sufficient for OTA performance.
- Competition is closed (no prize), but the leaderboard still accepts submissions for scoring.

## Acceptance criteria

1. **Ingest pipeline**:
   - Script to download dataset (Kaggle CLI auth required) under `data/cw-samples/kaggle-morse-v2/` (gitignored).
   - Manifest at `experiments/cw-decoder/scripts/kaggle_morse_v2/manifest.jsonl` mapping file -> truth (where labeled).
   - Reuse the existing `bench.py` harness; emit per-file CER + aggregate stats.

2. **Baseline run**: Score current best (viterbi from PR #411 + wpm-seed-fix from PR #423) on the 100 labeled training samples. Report mean / median / p95 CER, broken down by SNR bucket and WPM bucket.

3. **Submission**: Generate a submission CSV from the 100 unlabeled validation samples and submit to the leaderboard. Capture the leaderboard score in the report.

4. **Distribution cross-validation** (depends on `augment-arrl` landing): overlay our augmented corpus distributions against Kaggle's per-file (SNR, WPM, pitch) statistics. Flag any mismatch.

5. **Regression check**: confirm the PR #423 wpm-seed-fix gate behaves correctly at high WPM (50-80). Specifically check:
   - Is the histogram bias correction (`frame_len + frame_step` ≈ 35 ms) still appropriate at 80 WPM dit length (~15 ms)?
   - Does the dit/dah concentration gate fire correctly when both clusters are sub-30 ms?

6. **Honest report** with:
   - Per-SNR-bucket CER table
   - Per-WPM-bucket CER table
   - Failure-mode analysis on the worst 10 files (paste decoded vs truth)
   - Comparison: our score vs published `talengu/kaggle_morse` baseline (CNN+LSTM, ~2018-era)
   - Recommendation: any concrete decoder changes needed to reduce the high-WPM or low-SNR error rate

## Sequencing

This depends on:
- PR #411 (viterbi) and PR #423 (wpm-seed-fix) merged so we have a stable best-of-bake-off baseline to evaluate
- `augment-arrl` (PR TBD) for the distribution cross-validation step

Can begin ingest + baseline run as soon as #411 and #423 land. Distribution check waits on `augment-arrl`.

## Risks

- **Kaggle ToS**: dataset license must be checked before redistributing or training models from it. Likely "competition use only" — that's fine for in-repo benchmarking, but flag for the LLM-repair experiment (#422) which would consume training pairs.
- **Kaggle CLI auth**: requires per-developer Kaggle API token. Document setup in the script.
- **Dataset is synthetic**: do not over-weight Kaggle results — they validate decoder robustness across SNR/WPM but tell us nothing about Watterson channel, QRM, or fist variation.

## Open design questions

1. Submit to the leaderboard? It's public and our score becomes visible. Probably yes — gives us a citation-grade external number.
2. Use the 100 labeled files as additional regression bench, or hold them out for distribution validation only?
3. The published `talengu/kaggle_morse` baseline uses CNN+LSTM. Worth mining for ideas / weights / architecture before our `augment-arrl` + neural work?
title: experiment: ingest Kaggle Morse Learning Machine Challenge v2 as external benchmark

## Tool Type
Custom CLI tool (Node/Deno)

## Purpose
Give agents structured access to Kaggle — the data science competition platform and community. Kaggle provides active competitions (what problems the ML community is working on right now), trending notebooks (how people are solving them), and datasets.

## API
- **Kaggle API**: https://www.kaggle.com/docs/api — REST-based
- **Authentication**: API token required (free, from kaggle.com/settings)
- **Existing CLI**: \`kaggle\` Python CLI exists but is Python-only and focused on download/submission
- **Public data**: Competition listings, public notebooks, public datasets

## CLI Interface (proposed)

\`\`\`bash
# Competitions
kaggle competitions                  # Active competitions
kaggle competition <slug>            # Competition details + description
kaggle leaderboard <slug>            # Competition leaderboard
kaggle leaderboard <slug> --limit 20 # Top N entries

# Notebooks
kaggle notebooks --sort trending     # Trending notebooks
kaggle notebooks --competition <slug>  # Notebooks for a competition
kaggle notebook <slug>               # Notebook details + metadata

# Datasets
kaggle datasets --sort trending      # Trending datasets
kaggle datasets --search "query"     # Search datasets
kaggle dataset <slug>                # Dataset details + columns + preview

# Search
kaggle search "query"                # Search across competitions, notebooks, datasets
kaggle search "query" --type notebook

# Discovery
kaggle topics                        # Discussion topics/forums
kaggle discussion <id>               # Read discussion thread
kaggle user <username>               # User profile + tier + medals
\`\`\`

## Output Format
- **YAML** for all structured output
- Competition metadata: title, description, deadline, reward, team count, evaluation metric, tags
- Notebook metadata: title, author, votes, language (Python/R), competition link, last run date
- Dataset metadata: title, creator, size, download count, columns, usability score
- User metadata: username, tier (Grandmaster/Master/etc.), medals, competition ranking

## Key Design Decisions
1. **Competition-centric**: Competitions are Kaggle's unique signal — what ML problems have prizes and deadlines right now.
2. **Tier/medal system as signal**: Kaggle's ranking system (Grandmaster → Novice) indicates expertise. Surface it.
3. **No data download**: Discovery tool, not a data pipeline. Show metadata, schemas, and previews — not full datasets.
4. **API token required**: Setup instructions in CLAUDE.md.

## CLAUDE.md Content
- Kaggle as the ML competition platform — what problems are being solved and how
- Competition lifecycle: launch → join → submit → leaderboard → end
- Tier system and what each tier means for expertise signal
- Notebooks as shared solutions — the Kaggle community's knowledge base
- Datasets as structured data discovery
- Using Kaggle for "how do people solve X?" research

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] CLI is implemented in Node or Deno
- [ ] All output is YAML
- [ ] Competition listing and details work
- [ ] Notebook browsing works
- [ ] Dataset metadata and preview work
- [ ] \`tools/kaggle/CLAUDE.md\` covers discovery patterns
- [ ] Tests cover all subcommands
title: Kaggle — Custom CLI Tool

Rookies

**Project Title:**  
Green Point System for a Sustainable Campus

**Problem Statement Addressed:**  
College campuses often struggle to engage students in sustainability efforts, with no effective system to motivate, track, or reward eco-friendly actions. How can technology be used to create an engaging, transparent, and rewarding platform that encourages consistent student participation in building a greener campus?

**Project Overview:**  
The Green Point System is a tech-enabled, year-round program designed to make sustainability fun and rewarding on campus. Students earn points for participating in eco-friendly activities—such as waste collection, awareness campaigns, and green events—which are verified by campus volunteers. Achievements are recognized with digital badges and prizes, fostering friendly competition and long-term positive habits. The system will feature a mobile or web app for real-time activity logging, transparent leaderboards, and easy participation. MySky and DACs are our latest innovations in the Skynet app ecosystem. Building on the incredible power of SkyDB, MySky lets a user track and access their data across any Skynet App with a single login. This enables a new file and permissions system across Skynet, improving the experience of users and developers alike. DACs build on this, allowing developers to build on shared resources using exposed APIs -- all without worrying that another application's code might ruin your data.

Your hackathon project should utilize MySky and the Content Record DAC, which will allow users to submit their activities to our leaderboard. Prizes will be awarded in Siacoins, as determined by the exchange rate on the morning of the announcement.

# 🏆 Automatic Challenge Judging System Implementation

## Overview
Implemented a fully automated, secure challenge judging system with automatic credit distribution and comprehensive security features. The system processes challenges automatically when they end, awards winners based on ranking, and distributes prize pools without any manual intervention.

## 🎯 Key Features Implemented

### 1. **Automatic Processing**
- ✅ pg_cron job runs every 5 minutes to process ended challenges
- ✅ Immediate trigger when challenge `ends_at` timestamp is reached
- ✅ Challenges automatically transition from `active` to `archived` status
- ✅ No user intervention required - fully server-side automation

### 2. **Prize Distribution Algorithm**
- ✅ Configurable prize pool per challenge
- ✅ Top 3 winners receive: 50%, 30%, 20% of prize pool
- ✅ Support for configurable max_winners parameter
- ✅ Automatic credit allocation to winner profiles

### 3. **Database Schema Updates**

#### Tables Modified:
- `challenges` - Added: `ends_at`, `prize_pool`, `max_winners`, `auto_judge`, `judged_at`
- `challenge_submissions` - Added: `final_rank`, `credits_awarded`, `judged_at`
- `challenge_winners` - Created new table for winner records
- `credit_transactions` - Integrated for audit trail

#### Key Functions:
```sql
-- Main processing function
process_ended_challenges_direct()

-- Manual trigger for testing
manual_end_challenge(challenge_id UUID)

-- Eligibility checker
check_submission_eligibility(challenge_id UUID, user_id UUID)
```

### 4. **Security Implementation**

#### Row Level Security (RLS):
- ✅ Enabled on `challenges`, `challenge_submissions`, `challenge_winners`
- ✅ Users can only view their own submissions
- ✅ Winners visible only for completed challenges
- ✅ Submission validation prevents multiple entries

#### Validation Triggers:
- ✅ `validate_submission_trigger` - Prevents submissions to ended challenges
- ✅ `auto_judge_on_end_trigger` - Triggers processing when challenge ends
- ✅ Check constraints on difficulty, status, and other fields

### 5. **Credit System Integration**
- ✅ Automatic credit balance updates
- ✅ Transaction logging with type 'bonus' for rewards
- ✅ Full audit trail with metadata

[kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions) is a company that runs predictive modelling competitions on behalf of organisations. Competitors are given a dataset with covariates and response variables which they can use to train a model; they then use the model to make predictions for a new dataset (for which they only have the predictors, not the response variables) and submit these predictions to a web platform. The web platform compares the predictions with the withheld data and posts a score on a [leaderboard](https://www.kaggle.com/c/dog-breed-identification/leaderboard). At the end of the competition, the winner gets a prize and the organisation gets the model and code to produce it. It's pretty cool.

Predictive modelling competitions are also really useful to organisations and research communities that don't have the funds to use Kaggle or [similar commercial platforms](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/11142/sites-for-predictive-modeling-competitions), e.g. for resolving disputes about methodology (something I want to do with [zoon](https://ropensci.org/blog/blog/2016/12/12/ropensci-fellowship-zoon)), or for education (I have run something similar in an undergrad practical session). An R package that makes it easy to set up simple, free, self-hosted competitions like this could be really handy.

The main technical requirement is setting up a server (just an r session running on a web-connected computer) to host the hidden validation dataset, calculate the evaluation scores for each new submission, and serve a leaderboard on the web. The package could use [plumber](https://github.com/trestletech/plumber) (or [jug](http://bart6114.github.io/jug/index.html) or [OpenCPU](https://www.opencpu.org/) or something) to create the API for submission, create a shiny app for the leaderboard and to host the training data to download, and provide users with streamlined functions to submit predictions.

So the organiser might do something like:
```r
run_competition(title = "predict the weights of these guinea pigs",
                description = "build a model that predicts the weights of these loveable balls of
                               fluff from some metadata about them",
                training_data = "train_guinea_pig_features_weights.Rdata",
                test_data = "test_guinea_pig_features.rds"
                secret_test_labels = "test_guinea_pig_weights.csv",
                metric = "RMSE")
```
```
Your competition and leaderboard is live and hosted at:
  http://128.250.4.119/8000
```

Competitors could also use the package to submit their predictions to the leaderboard:
```r
submit_prediction(predicted_weights,
                  website = "http://128.250.4.119/8000",
                  user = "nick",
                  password = "averysecurepassword1")
```

### metaMirage (CognitiveMirage) — DEADLINE April 16 2026
**Commits (24h):** 8 (7 substantive + 1 daily report)
**Lines changed:** est. +1,400 (new scripts, data files, blog post, HF Space, dashboard section, README expansion)
**Key finding / progress:**

Submission package finalized and hardened with six analytical additions beyond the April 14 report:

1. **Robustness sensitivity** (`v3_sensitivity.py`) — 94% of 36 (w_rubric, w_abstain, w_expert) triplets on a 0.1-grid yield negative r; 81% reach p < 0.05. Median r = −0.82, canonical r = −0.841. Sign flips only at extreme expert-weight corners (w_expert ≥ 0.8). Defends Weakness #5.

2. **Novelty/contamination audit** (`v3_novelty_audit.py`) — char-5-gram Jaccard vs 30 MMLU-style probes: max = 0.275, mean = 0.051, median = 0.033; 1/50 tasks above the 0.20 threshold. Tasks are demonstrably not MMLU rephrasings.

3. **Item discrimination** (`v3_item_discrimination.py`) — 10/50 tasks have model-spread ≥ 0.3 across 3 Anthropic models; 16/50 ≥ 0.1; control tasks uniform at spread = 0 (expected). Defends dataset quality at item level.

4. **Absolute calibration** (`v3_calibration.py`) — Brier score + ECE (5 bins) on Anthropic subset:

   | Model | Brier | ECE | Brier (clean) | Brier (mirage) |
   |-------|-------|-----|---------------|----------------|
   | haiku-4-5 | 0.201 | 0.297 | 0.01 | 0.40 |
   | opus-4-5  | 0.221 | 0.307 | 0.01 | 0.45 |
   | sonnet-4-5 | 0.224 | 0.314 | 0.01 | 0.45 |

   Brier gap (0.01 clean → ~0.45 mirage) mirrors TDR collapse — models are well-calibrated on clean questions but overconfidently miscalibrated on mirages.

5. **Public presence** — `BLOG_POST.md` (800-word post; r = −0.84 + within-Anthropic Opus 4.0→4.5 monitoring collapse as grand-prize novelty angle), `hf_space/` (Gradio app; visitor plugs in API key, runs 5–20 tasks, sees results vs published leaderboard), `TWEET_THREAD.md` (8-tweet template), `v3_local_eval.py` (Ollama-backed; Llama-3.2 evaluation running; Qwen-2.5-3B pulled and ready — adds open-weight models to pool at zero API cost).

6. **Dashboard Robustness & Validity section** (7th section, `feat(dashboard)` commit):
   - 3-stat strip: permutation p = 0.023, cross-judge r = 0.88, 94% weight sensitivity
   - Bootstrap 95% CI table (5 correlations × 4 cols: r, CI, perm p, excludes-zero)

# 🎨 ShutterScore - Complete Project Overview

## What You've Got

A **production-ready, monetized photo contest platform** that uses AI to judge photos instantly. Users pay $1.25 per entry, AI scores them out of 40 points, and the highest score wins $500.

## 💰 Business Model

**Revenue Streams:**
1. **Entry Fees**: $1.25 per photo submission
2. **Future**: Premium subscriptions, sponsored contests, featured placements

**Cost Structure:**
- OpenAI API: ~$0.02 per photo scored
- Vercel hosting: $0-20/month (free tier available)
- Database: $0-19/month (Neon free tier)
- Stripe fees: 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction
- **Net margin: ~95% on entry fees**

**Example: 1000 entries/month**
- Revenue: $1,250
- Costs: ~$65
- **Profit: ~$1,185/month**

## 🎯 Key Features

### For Users
- ✅ One-click Google sign-in
- ✅ Upload photos instantly ($1.25/entry)
- ✅ AI judges in 10-30 seconds
- ✅ Detailed scores (Technical, Composition, Impact, Originality)
- ✅ Live leaderboard with rankings
- ✅ Personal dashboard with all entries
- ✅ Achievement badges and points system
- ✅ Real $500 prize for winners

### For You (Admin)
- ✅ Automated contest management
- ✅ Zero manual judging required
- ✅ Stripe payment processing
- ✅ User analytics built-in
- ✅ Easy to create new contests
- ✅ Scalable infrastructure

## 🛠️ Technology Stack

- **Frontend**: Next.js 14, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
- **Backend**: Next.js API Routes, Prisma ORM
- **Database**: PostgreSQL (any provider)
- **Auth**: NextAuth.js (Google OAuth)
- **Storage**: Vercel Blob (for photos)
- **AI**: OpenAI GPT-4 Vision API
- **Payments**: Stripe
- **Hosting**: Vercel
- **Analytics**: Vercel Analytics

## 📁 Project Structure

```
shutterscore/
├── app/
│   ├── page.tsx              # Landing page (stunning design)
│   ├── contest/
│   │   ├── page.tsx          # Contest entry page
│   │   └── UploadForm.tsx    # Photo upload component
│   ├── leaderboard/
│   │   └── page.tsx          # Rankings page
│   ├── me/
│   │   └── page.tsx          # User profile/dashboard
│   ├── api/
│   │   ├── auth/             # NextAuth routes
│   │   ├── entries/
│   │   │   ├── upload/       # Photo upload endpoint
│   │   │   └── score/        # AI scoring endpoint
│   │   └── checkout/         # Stripe payment
│   ├── layout.tsx            # Root layout
│   ├── providers.tsx         # Auth provider
│   └── globals.css           # Global styles
├── lib/
│   ├── auth.ts               # NextAuth config
│   └── prisma.ts             # Database client
├── prisma/
│   ├── schema.prisma         # Database schema
│   └── seed.ts               # Initial data
├── .env.example              # Environment template
├── README.md                 # Full documentation
├── QUICKSTART.md             # 5-minute setup guide
├── DEPLOYMENT.md             # Production deployment guide
└── setup.sh                  # Automated setup script
```

## 🚀 How to Launch (3 Options)

### Option 1: Quick Local Test (5 minutes)
```bash
cd shutterscore
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local
# Edit .env.local with your keys
npx prisma db push
npx prisma db seed
npm run dev
```

### Option 2: Deploy to Vercel (15 minutes)
1. Push to GitHub
2. Import to Vercel
3. Add environment variables
4. Deploy
5. See DEPLOYMENT.md for details

### Option 3: Automated Setup (2 minutes)
```bash
cd shutterscore
chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh
# Edit .env.local
npm run dev
```

## 🎨 Design Highlights

The UI features a **bold, modern aesthetic**:

- **Dark gradient backgrounds** (slate → purple → slate)
- **Animated glowing orbs** for depth and movement
- **Yellow/orange CTAs** for maximum conversion
- **Glass-morphism cards** with backdrop blur
- **Smooth transitions** and micro-interactions
- **Mobile-first** responsive design
- **Professional typography** and spacing

**No generic AI slop** - this is custom-designed for engagement!

## 📊 Core User Flow

1. **Discover** → Land on homepage, see active contest
2. **Sign Up** → One-click Google OAuth
3. **Enter** → Upload photo, pay $1.25 via Stripe
4. **Wait** → AI scores photo in 10-30 seconds
5. **View Results** → See detailed score breakdown
6. **Check Leaderboard** → Compare with other entries
7. **Win** → Top score gets $500 prize

## 💳 Payment Integration

**Stripe Checkout** handles all payments:
- PCI-compliant (you never touch card data)
- Test mode included (test cards work)
- Automatic receipts
- Webhook for payment confirmation
- Easy to switch to live mode

**Test Card**: `4242 4242 4242 4242` (any expiry/CVC)

## 🤖 AI Scoring System

Uses **OpenAI GPT-4 Vision** to analyze photos:

1. Photo uploaded to Vercel Blob
2. API sends image + scoring prompt to GPT-4
3. AI returns JSON with 4 scores (0-10 each):
   - **Technical**: Exposure, focus, lighting, color
   - **Composition**: Framing, balance, rule of thirds
   - **Impact**: Emotional response, wow factor
   - **Originality**: Creativity, unique perspective
4. Total score (0-40) saved to database
5. Leaderboard updates instantly

**Cost**: ~$0.02 per image scored

## 📈 Monetization Strategy

### Phase 1: Entry Fees (Now)
- $1.25 per photo entry
- 95% profit margin
- Scales linearly with users

### Phase 2: Premium (Month 2)
- $9.99/month for unlimited entries
- Additional features (analytics, coaching)
- Recurring revenue

### Phase 3: Sponsored Contests (Month 3)
- Brands pay to host custom contests
- Bigger prize pools ($1000+)
- B2B revenue stream

### Phase 4: Featured Placements (Month 6)
- Users pay to promote their photos
- Front-page placement
- Additional revenue per user

## 🎯 Target Market

**Primary**: Amateur photographers
- Age 25-45
- Smartphone and DSLR users
- Active on Instagram/500px
- Willing to pay for feedback
- Competitive mindset

**Secondary**: Photo enthusiasts
- Hobbyists wanting to improve
- Users seeking validation
- Social media creators

**Market Size**: 
- 95M amateur photographers in US
- 1.5B smartphone photographers globally
- $10B+ photography contest market

## 📊 Success Metrics

**Week 1 Goals:**
- 100 sign-ups
- 50 paid entries
- $62.50 revenue

**Month 1 Goals:**
- 500 sign-ups
- 300 paid entries
- $375 revenue
- Break even on costs

**Month 3 Goals:**
- 5,000 sign-ups
- 2,000 paid entries
- $2,500 revenue
- Launch premium tier

## 🔧 Customization Ideas

**Easy Wins:**
1. Change contest theme (urban, nature, portrait, etc.)
2. Adjust prize amounts ($100, $1000, etc.)
3. Modify entry price ($0.99, $2.99, etc.)
4. Add more achievements
5. Customize color scheme

**Advanced:**
1. Add community voting (combo AI + human)
2. Multi-contest system
3. Social sharing features
4. Photo editing tools
5. Mobile app (React Native)

## 🚨 Important Notes

### Before Going Live:

1. **Legal**:
   - Add Terms of Service page
   - Add Privacy Policy page
   - Contest rules and disclaimers
   - Prize payout terms

2. **Stripe**:
   - Switch from test to live mode
   - Set up webhook in production
   - Verify payout account

3. **Marketing**:
   - Landing page SEO
   - Social media accounts
   - Email collection
   - Launch campaign

4. **Support**:
   - Support email setup
   - FAQ page
   - Contact form
   - Refund policy

## 📚 Documentation Included

1. **README.md** - Full project documentation
2. **QUICKSTART.md** - 5-minute setup guide
3. **DEPLOYMENT.md** - Production deployment guide
4. **This file** - Business overview

## 🎓 What You've Learned

This project demonstrates:
- ✅ Full-stack Next.js 14 development
- ✅ TypeScript best practices
- ✅ Prisma ORM and PostgreSQL
- ✅ NextAuth authentication
- ✅ OpenAI API integration
- ✅ Stripe payment processing
- ✅ Vercel deployment
- ✅ Modern UI/UX design
- ✅ SaaS business model

## 💡 Next Steps

1. **Set up locally** - Follow QUICKSTART.md
2. **Test everything** - Upload photos, check scoring
3. **Customize design** - Make it yours
4. **Deploy to Vercel** - Follow DEPLOYMENT.md

## 📈 Revenue Projections

## 🎉 You're Ready!

Everything you need to launch a monetized photo contest platform:

✅ Beautiful, engaging design
✅ AI-powered judging system

@claude please implement everything below on a new branch named `learn`. Open a single PR from `learn` to `main` when complete. Use four logical commits in order: (1) skeleton, (2) AXL, (3) 0G, (4) demo.

## Project goal

Build a decentralized population-based training system for a backgammon RL agent. Each node trains its own agent via self-play, discovers peers over AXL (Gensyn's P2P network), challenges them to matches, and exchanges checkpoints. Agent weights persist to 0G Storage. Match results post to an ELO leaderboard contract on 0G Chain. Submission target: ETHGlobal Open Agents (Gensyn AXL prize + 0G Autonomous Agents/Swarms prize).

## Why backgammon

Clean benchmark domain. Stochastic (dice) so it suits population-based methods. gnubg exists as an objective external evaluator (we'll wire that up in a later PR). The classic TD-Gammon result (Tesauro 1992) shows a small MLP trained via TD(λ) self-play reaches strong play, so the compute budget is hackathon-friendly.

## Commit 1: skeleton (`backgammon/`)

Create the following modules. Keep the core training loop pure Python + PyTorch, no network deps.

### `backgammon/env.py`
- Board state: 24 points (signed integers, +White/-Black), bar[2], off[2], turn.
- `starting_state()`: standard opening — White 2 on point 0, 5 on 11, 3 on 16, 5 on 18; Black mirrored.
- White moves 0→23, bears off from 18-23. Black moves 23→0, bears off from 0-5.
- `legal_move_sequences(state, dice) -> list[(resulting_state, [(src,die), ...])]`
  - Doubles play four times.
  - Must enter from bar before any other move.
  - Must use as many dice as possible; if only one playable, must play the larger die when possible.
  - Bear-off: all checkers in home board; exact roll, or larger roll only if no checkers behind.
  - Hit blot: opponent checker alone on a point goes to bar.
- `is_terminal(state)`, `game_outcome(state) -> (winner, multiplier)` where multiplier is 1=single, 2=gammon (loser borne off 0), 3=backgammon (loser still on bar or in winner's home board).

### `backgammon/encode.py`
- TD-Gammon 198-feature encoding: per (24 points × 2 players × 4 features) = 192, plus [bar_W/2, off_W/15, bar_B/2, off_B/15, turn==W, turn==B]. The 4 per-point features are: (≥1, ≥2, ≥3, max(0, n-3)/2).

### `backgammon/net.py`
- Small MLP: 198 → hidden (default 128) → hidden → 4, sigmoid out.
- Cumulative-head outputs: [P(W wins any), P(W wins gammon+), P(B wins any), P(B wins gammon+)].
- White equity helper: (out[0] + out[1]) − (out[2] + out[3]).

### `backgammon/agent.py`
- `NetAgent(net, epsilon)`: enumerate legal sequences, encode each resulting state, score from mover's perspective (negate equity if Black to move), argmax. Epsilon-random for exploration.
- `RandomAgent` baseline.

### `backgammon/selfplay.py`
- `play_game(white_agent, black_agent, rng_py, rng_np) -> Trajectory` containing the encoded states visited and the terminal 4-vector target.
- Opening roll: re-roll until non-doubles; higher die plays first.
- `td_lambda_update(net, optimizer, traj, lam=0.7)`: backward sweep computing λ-returns toward terminal target, MSE loss, single optimizer step.

### `backgammon/train.py`
- CLI flags: `--epochs`, `--games-per-epoch`, `--lr`, `--lambda-td`, `--epsilon`, `--hidden`, `--seed`, `--ckpt-dir`.
- Per epoch: run N self-play games, TD update after each, evaluate vs RandomAgent (alternating sides), save checkpoint.
- Print `epoch | avg_moves | loss | win_rate_vs_random | time`.

### Tests (`tests/`)
- `test_env.py`: starting position has 15+15 checkers; checker conservation across 50 random rollouts; all rollouts terminate; specific roll (3,1) from start gives ≥10 candidate sequences.
- `test_net.py`: forward pass shape; equity calculation symmetric.

### Acceptance for commit 1
`python -m backgammon.train --epochs 5 --games-per-epoch 100` runs to completion and shows `vs_random` rising above 0.7 by epoch 5.

## Commit 2: AXL coordination (`backgammon/axl/`)

AXL is a P2P node binary that exposes encrypted mesh communication via localhost HTTP. Docs: https://docs.gensyn.ai/tech/agent-exchange-layer. Reference: https://github.com/gensyn-ai/axl. Verify the actual API before implementing — if it differs from what's described here, comment on this issue with the proposed adaptation rather than guessing.

### `backgammon/axl/messages.py`
Dataclasses with `to_dict`/`from_dict`:
- `ANNOUNCE {agent_id, checkpoint_hash, elo, generation}`
- `CHALLENGE {from_id, n_games, seed}`
- `MATCH_RESULT {agent_a, agent_b, score_a, score_b, n_games}`
- `WEIGHTS_REQ {checkpoint_hash}`
- `WEIGHTS_RESP {checkpoint_hash, storage_uri}` (just the URI; bytes live on 0G — see commit 3)

### `backgammon/axl/node.py`
- Wraps a single training agent.
- Background thread runs self-play training continuously.
- HTTP server on the AXL-assigned localhost port handles incoming messages.
- Every K minutes (configurable, default 2): announce checkpoint, pick a peer, challenge for 20 games, update local ELO (K-factor 32), if peer ELO exceeds self by 50+ points pull weights and replace.
- Peer pool: max 10, LRU eviction.
- Entry point: `python -m backgammon.axl.node --peers <id1,id2,...> [--no-chain] [--no-storage]`.

### Tests
- `test_axl_messages.py`: every message type round-trips through serialization.
- `test_axl_node.py`: two in-process nodes (mocked AXL transport) exchange one full match cycle, both update ELO consistently.

## Commit 3: 0G Storage + Chain (`backgammon/og/`, `contracts/`)

0G has Storage (decentralized blob store), Compute, and an EVM chain. We use Storage and Chain only. Builder hub: https://build.0g.ai. Verify SDK names/imports before implementing.

### `backgammon/og/storage.py`
- `upload_checkpoint(state_dict) -> str`: serialize state_dict, upload to 0G Storage, return URI.
- `download_checkpoint(uri) -> state_dict`.
- `upload_game_record(trajectory) -> str`.
- Storage key: `sha256(weights_bytes)` for checkpoints — content-addressed, deduplicates across nodes.

### `backgammon/og/chain.py`
- Web3.py client for the Tournament contract.
- Reads the deployed contract address from `deployments/0g_testnet.json` (do not hardcode).
- `report_match(agent_a, agent_b, score_a, sig_a, sig_b) -> tx_hash`.
- `get_elo(agent) -> int`.
- `top_n(n) -> list[(address, elo)]`.

### `contracts/Tournament.sol`
- Solidity ^0.8.20.
- Mapping `address => int32` ELO ratings, default 1500.
- `reportMatch(address a, address b, uint8 score_a, uint8 score_b, bytes sigA, bytes sigB)`:
  - Verify both signatures are EIP-712 over `(a, b, score_a, score_b, nonce)`.
  - Replay protection via incrementing per-pair nonce.
  - Update ELO with K-factor 32.
  - Emit `MatchReported(address a, address b, uint8 winner, int32 newEloA, int32 newEloB)`.
- `topN(uint256 n)` view function returning sorted leaderboard.

### Hardhat setup
- `hardhat.config.js` with Solidity 0.8.20, optimizer enabled (200 runs), and a `0g_testnet` network entry (RPC URL from `OG_RPC_URL` env var, deployer key from `DEPLOYER_PRIVATE_KEY`).
- `package.json` pinning `hardhat`, `@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox`, `ethers`, `dotenv`.
- `scripts/deploy.js` deploys `Tournament` and writes the address + ABI path to `deployments/0g_testnet.json`.

### `test/Tournament.test.js`
Hardhat + ethers tests using `hardhat-toolbox` (chai matchers, network helpers). Cover:
- Happy path: valid co-signed match updates both ELOs symmetrically (sum preserved up to rounding).
- Missing signature reverts.
- Wrong-signer signature reverts.
- Replay attack (re-submitting same nonce) reverts.
- ELO drift: 100 mock matches between two equal-strength agents stays within ±50 of starting 1500 for both.

### Wire-through
- AXL `WEIGHTS_RESP` returns 0G Storage URI instead of inline bytes.
- After each AXL `MATCH_RESULT` exchange, both nodes co-sign (EIP-712) and one submits to chain.
- `backgammon/og/chain.py` loads the contract address from `deployments/0g_testnet.json`.

## Commit 4: end-to-end demo (`demo/`)

### `demo/run_local_swarm.sh`
Spin up 5 AXL nodes locally, each with: distinct seed, varied hyperparameters (sample `lambda_td ∈ {0.5, 0.7, 0.9}`, `lr ∈ {5e-4, 1e-3, 2e-3}`, `hidden ∈ {64, 128, 192}`). Pass each node the others' AXL IDs. Output logs to `demo/logs/node_N.log`.

### `demo/leaderboard.py`
Polls the chain every 30s, prints sorted leaderboard with deltas since last poll.

### `demo/README.md`
~200 words: what the demo shows, how to run (including `npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network 0g_testnet` as a prerequisite), what to look for in the logs (peer discovery, first match exchange, first chain submission, ELO divergence).

### `docs/architecture.md`
~300 words + a mermaid diagram showing the three layers (training core, AXL mesh, 0G persistence) and how a single match flows through them.

## Cross-cutting requirements

- **Don't break the standalone path.** `python -m backgammon.train` must still work without AXL or 0G.
- **Feature flags.** `--no-network` and `--no-chain` skip those layers cleanly. The demo without flags requires AXL/0G; with flags, just runs local self-play.
- **Type hints throughout.** `mypy backgammon/` should pass.
- **Pinned Python dependencies** in `requirements.txt`. Brief justification per dep in the PR description.
- **Pinned JS dependencies** in `package.json` (Hardhat, ethers, toolbox, dotenv).
- **No secrets in commits.** Provide `.env.example` covering `OG_RPC_URL`, `DEPLOYER_PRIVATE_KEY`, and any AXL-specific env vars.
- **Python 3.11+, Node 20+.**

## Acceptance checklist

- [ ] Branch `learn`, four ordered commits, single PR to `main`.
- [ ] Commit 1 alone runs end-to-end and learns vs random.
- [ ] `pytest tests/` passes.
- [ ] `npx hardhat compile` produces clean artifacts.
- [ ] `npx hardhat test` passes.
- [ ] `npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network hardhat` (local node) runs end-to-end and writes a deployment file. Document the command in the PR description.
- [ ] `mypy backgammon/` clean.
- [ ] `demo/run_local_swarm.sh` brings up 5 nodes that discover each other and exchange ≥1 match within 60s.
- [ ] PR description includes: architecture diagram, dependency list (Python + JS) with justification, known limitations, what's tested vs. only stubbed.

## Important: handling unknowns

The AXL and 0G SDKs may have changed since your training data. Before writing integration code in commits 2 and 3, fetch the current docs (linked above) and confirm the API surface. If the actual API differs materially from this spec, **comment on this issue with the discrepancy and your proposed adaptation, then wait for confirmation.** Don't paper over API mismatches with mocks.

If anything else is ambiguous, comment first rather than guessing.
