    "\n",
    "# Suppress warnings\n",
    "logging.getLogger(\"llama_cpp\").setLevel(logging.ERROR)\n",
    "\n",
    "# Determinism\n",
    "random.seed(42)\n",
    "np.random.seed(42)\n",
    "\n",
    "DEVICE = \"cuda\" if torch.cuda.is_available() else \"cpu\"\n",
    "\n",
    "# Constants\n",
    "TIMESTAMP = time.strftime(\"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S\")\n",
    "MODEL_PATH = \"/kaggle/input/sigilagi_models/llama-2-7b.Q4_K_M.gguf\"\n",
    "LLAVA_PATH = \"/kaggle/input/sigilagi_models/llava-v1.6-mistral-7b.Q2_K.gguf\"\n",
    "OBSERVER_MODEL_PATH = \"/kaggle/input/sigilagi_models/distilbert-base-uncased\"\n",
    "NUM_PROCESSES = min(6, os.cpu_count() or 1)\n",
    "HARC_PRIORS = [\"symmetry\", \"fill_nonzero\", \"tile\", \"color_map\", \"pattern_repeat\", \"connect_components\", \"edge_detect\", \"color_remap\", \"preserve_shapes\"]\n",
    "\n",
    "# Setup Logger\n",
    "logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format=\"%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s\")\n",
    "logger = logging.getLogger(\"SIGILAGI_v5.2\")\n",
    "\n",
    "# --- Utility Functions ---\n",
    "\n",
    "def grid_to_image(grid: np.ndarray) -> Image.Image:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Converts grid to PIL Image.\"\"\"\n",
    "    cmap = np.array([\n",
    "        [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 255], [255, 0, 0], [0, 255, 0], [255, 255, 0],\n",
    "        [255, 0, 255], [0, 255, 255], [255, 128, 0], [128, 0, 255], [0, 128, 0]\n",
    "    ], dtype=np.uint8)\n",
    "    scale = 10\n",
    "    grid_rgb = cmap[grid % 10]\n",
    "    h, w, c = grid_rgb.shape\n",
    "    img = Image.fromarray(grid_rgb, 'RGB').resize((w * scale, h * scale), Image.NEAREST)\n",
    "    return img\n",
    "\n",
    "def parse_grid_from_output(output: str) -> np.ndarray | None:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Parses JSON grid from LLM output.\"\"\"\n",
    "    try:\n",
    "        start = output.find(\"[\")\n",
    "        end = output.rfind(\"]\") + 1\n",
    "        if start == -1 or end <= start:\n",
    "            raise ValueError(\"No valid JSON array found\")\n",
    "        json_str = output[start:end]\n",
    "        grid = np.array(json.loads(json_str), dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "        return grid\n",
    "    except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError) as e:\n",
    "        logger.error(f\"Parse failed: {e}\\nOutput: {output[:200]}...\")\n",
    "        return None\n",
    "\n",
    "# --- Rule Application ---\n",
    "\n",
    "def apply_rule(grid: np.ndarray, rule: str) -> np.ndarray:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Applies transformation rule with vectorized operations.\"\"\"\n",
    "    output = grid.astype(np.int8).copy()\n",
    "    h, w = grid.shape\n",
    "\n",
    "    if rule == \"copy_input\":\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "    if rule == \"rotate_90\":\n",
    "        return np.rot90(output, k=1)\n",
    "    if rule == \"flip_horizontal\":\n",
    "        return np.flip(output, axis=1)\n",
    "    if rule == \"mirror_vertical\" or rule == \"symmetry\":\n",
    "        return np.flip(output, axis=0)\n",
    "    if rule == \"diagonal_flip\":\n",
    "        return np.transpose(output)\n",
    "    if rule == \"color_swap\":\n",
    "        unique_colors = np.unique(output)\n",
    "        if len(unique_colors) > 1:\n",
    "            color_map = {c: unique_colors[-(i + 1)] for i, c in enumerate(unique_colors)}\n",
    "            vectorized_map = np.vectorize(color_map.get, otypes=[np.int8])\n",
    "            return vectorized_map(output)\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "    if rule == \"color_fill\":\n",
    "        colors, counts = np.unique(output[output != 0], return_counts=True)\n",
    "        if colors.size > 0:\n",
    "            return np.full_like(output, colors[np.argmax(counts)], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "    if rule == \"pattern_repeat\" or rule == \"tile\":\n",
    "        return np.tile(output, (2, 2)).astype(np.int8)\n",
    "    if rule == \"fill_gaps\":\n",
    "        mask = output == 0\n",
    "        neighbors = np.zeros_like(output, dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "        for di, dj in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]:\n",
    "            rolled = np.roll(output, (di, dj), axis=(0, 1))\n",
    "            valid = (rolled != 0) & mask\n",
    "            neighbors[valid] = 1\n",
    "        output[mask & (neighbors > 0)] = 1\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "    if rule == \"connect_components\":\n",
    "        output[output != 0] = 1\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "    if rule == \"fill_nonzero\":\n",
    "        output[output != 0] = 1\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "    if rule == \"color_map\":\n",
    "        unique = np.unique(output)\n",
    "        remap = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(unique)}\n",
    "        return np.vectorize(remap.get, otypes=[np.int8])(output)\n",
    "    if rule == \"edge_detect\":\n",
    "        gx = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=np.float32)\n",
    "        gy = np.array([[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]], dtype=np.float32)\n",
    "        edges_x = np.zeros_like(output, dtype=np.float32)\n",
    "        edges_y = np.zeros_like(output, dtype=np.float32)\n",
    "        for i in range(1, h-1):\n",
    "            for j in range(1, w-1):\n",
    "                edges_x[i, j] = np.sum(output[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2] * gx)\n",
    "                edges_y[i, j] = np.sum(output[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2] * gy)\n",
    "        edges = np.sqrt(edges_x**2 + edges_y**2)\n",
    "        return (edges > np.mean(edges) * 1.5).astype(np.int8) * output\n",
    "    if rule.startswith(\"tile_subgrid_\"):\n",
    "        sh, sw = map(int, rule.split(\"_\")[-1].split(\"x\"))\n",
    "        subgrid = output[:sh, :sw]\n",
    "        return np.tile(subgrid, (h // sh, w // sw)).astype(np.int8)\n",
    "    if rule == \"scale_2x\":\n",
    "        return np.repeat(np.repeat(output, 2, axis=0), 2, axis=1).astype(np.int8)\n",
    "\n",
    "    logger.warning(f\"Rule '{rule}' not implemented.\")\n",
    "    return output\n",
    "\n",
    "def apply_multi_step(grid: np.ndarray, rule_sequence: list) -> np.ndarray:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Applies rule sequence with memoization.\"\"\"\n",
    "    output = grid.astype(np.int8).copy()\n",
    "    memo = {}\n",
    "    for rule in rule_sequence:\n",
    "        key = (zlib.crc32(output.tobytes()), rule)\n",
    "        if key in memo:\n",
    "            output = memo[key]\n",
    "        else:\n",
    "            output = apply_rule(output, rule)\n",
    "            memo[key] = output\n",
    "    return output\n",
    "\n",
    "# --- Caching ---\n",
    "\n",
    "class RuleResultCache:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Compressed LRU cache with zlib.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self, capacity: int = 1000):\n",
    "        self.cache = OrderedDict()\n",
    "        self.capacity = max(500, int(psutil.virtual_memory().available / (1024**2 * 10)))\n",
    "        self.pre_cache_common_grids()\n",
    "\n",
    "    def pre_cache_common_grids(self):\n",
    "        common_grids = [np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=np.int8), np.ones((5, 5), dtype=np.int8)]\n",
    "        rules = [\"rotate_90\", \"color_swap\", \"tile\", \"color_remap\"]\n",
    "        for grid in common_grids:\n",
    "            for rule in rules:\n",
    "                self.set(grid, rule, apply_rule(grid, rule))\n",
    "\n",
    "    def get(self, grid: np.ndarray, rule: str) -> np.ndarray | None:\n",
    "        key = (zlib.crc32(grid.tobytes()), rule)\n",
    "        if key in self.cache:\n",
    "            self.cache.move_to_end(key)\n",
    "            return self.cache[key]\n",
    "        return None\n",
    "\n",
    "    def set(self, grid: np.ndarray, rule: str, result: np.ndarray):\n",
    "        if np.array_equal(grid, result):\n",
    "            return\n",
    "        key = (zlib.crc32(grid.tobytes()), rule)\n",
    "        self.cache[key] = result.astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        self.cache.move_to_end(key)\n",
    "        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:\n",
    "            self.cache.popitem(last=False)\n",
    "\n",
    "class LRUCache:\n",
    "    \"\"\"LRU cache for LLaVA.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self, capacity: int = 100):\n",
    "        self.cache = OrderedDict()\n",
    "        self.capacity = capacity\n",
    "\n",
    "    def get(self, state_key: tuple) -> np.ndarray | None:\n",
    "        if state_key in self.cache:\n",
    "            self.cache.move_to_end(state_key)\n",
    "            return self.cache[state_key]\n",
    "        return None\n",
    "\n",
    "    def set(self, state_key: tuple, result: np.ndarray):\n",
    "        self.cache[state_key] = result.astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        self.cache.move_to_end(state_key)\n",
    "        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:\n",
    "            self.cache.popitem(last=False)\n",
    "\n",
    "# --- Components ---\n",
    "\n",
    "class VisionLattice:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized feature extraction.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self):\n",
    "        self.feature_cache = {}\n",
    "        self.cache_capacity = max(500, int(psutil.virtual_memory().available / (1024**2 * 5)))\n",
    "\n",
    "    def process_frame(self, grid):\n",
    "        cache_key = zlib.crc32(grid.tobytes())\n",
    "        if cache_key in self.feature_cache:\n",
    "            return self.feature_cache[cache_key]\n",
    "\n",
    "        arr = grid.astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        if not arr.size:\n",
    "            return {}\n",
    "\n",
    "        h, w = arr.shape\n",
    "        v_sym = np.mean(arr[:, :w//2] == np.fliplr(arr[:, :w//2])) if w >= 4 else 1.0\n",
    "        h_sym = np.mean(arr[:h//2, :] == np.flipud(arr[:h//2, :])) if h >= 4 else 1.0\n",
    "        density = (arr != 0).sum() / arr.size\n",
    "        edges = np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(arr, axis=0)) + np.abs(np.diff(arr, axis=1))) / max(1, (h * w * 2))\n",
    "        _, num_objects = label(arr)\n",
    "        freq = np.abs(fft2(arr, norm=\"forward\")).mean() if arr.size >= 4 else 0.0\n",
    "        repeating = freq > np.mean(arr) * 1.2\n",
    "\n",
    "        features = {\n",
    "            \"harc_priors\": {\n",
    "                \"symmetry\": v_sym > 0.8 or h_sym > 0.8,\n",
    "                \"fill_nonzero\": density > 0.3,\n",
    "                \"tile\": (h % 2 == 0 and w % 2 == 0) or repeating,\n",
    "                \"color_map\": len(np.unique(arr)) >= 3,\n",
    "                \"pattern_repeat\": density > 0.5 or repeating,\n",
    "                \"connect_components\": num_objects > 2,\n",
    "                \"edge_detect\": edges > 0.1,\n",
    "                \"color_remap\": len(np.unique(arr)) >= 2,\n",
    "                \"preserve_shapes\": num_objects > 0\n",
    "            },\n",
    "            \"symmetry_score\": max(v_sym, h_sym),\n",
    "            \"density\": density,\n",
    "            \"edge_density\": edges,\n",
    "            \"num_objects\": num_objects,\n",
    "            \"frequency_score\": freq\n",
    "        }\n",
    "        self.feature_cache[cache_key] = features\n",
    "        if len(self.feature_cache) > self.cache_capacity:\n",
    "            self.feature_cache.pop(list(self.feature_cache.keys())[0])\n",
    "        return features\n",
    "\n",
    "    def detect_patterns(self, input_grid: np.ndarray, output_grid: np.ndarray) -> List[str]:\n",
    "        \"\"\"Optimized pattern induction.\"\"\"\n",
    "        rules = []\n",
    "        input_grid = input_grid.astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        output_grid = output_grid.astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        h, w = input_grid.shape\n",
    "        h_out, w_out = output_grid.shape\n",
    "\n",
    "        for sh in range(1, min(h // 2 + 1, 3)):\n",
    "            for sw in range(1, min(w // 2 + 1, 3)):\n",
    "                subgrid = input_grid[:sh, :sw]\n",
    "                if h % sh == 0 and w % sw == 0:\n",
    "                    tiled = np.tile(subgrid, (h // sh, w // sw))\n",
    "                    if np.array_equal(tiled, output_grid):\n",
    "                        rules.append(f\"tile_subgrid_{sh}x{sw}\")\n",
    "\n",
    "        unique_in, counts_in = np.unique(input_grid, return_counts=True)\n",
    "        unique_out, counts_out = np.unique(output_grid, return_counts=True)\n",
    "        if len(unique_in) == len(unique_out) and len(unique_in) <= 10:\n",
    "            color_map = {unique_in[i]: unique_out[i] for i in range(len(unique_in))}\n",
    "            mapped = np.vectorize(color_map.get, otypes=[np.int8])(input_grid)\n",
    "            if np.array_equal(mapped, output_grid):\n",
    "                rules.append(\"color_remap\")\n",
    "\n",
    "        _, num_in = label(input_grid)\n",
    "        _, num_out = label(output_grid)\n",
    "        if num_in == num_out:\n",
    "            rules.append(\"preserve_shapes\")\n",
    "\n",
    "        if h_out == h * 2 and w_out == w * 2:\n",
    "            scaled = np.repeat(np.repeat(input_grid, 2, axis=0), 2, axis=1)\n",
    "            if np.array_equal(scaled, output_grid):\n",
    "                rules.append(\"scale_2x\")\n",
    "\n",
    "        return rules\n",
    "\n",
    "class ARCObserver:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Rule suggestion with lazy LoRA loading.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self, rule_applier):\n",
    "        self.tokenizer = None\n",
    "        self.model = None\n",
    "        self.rule_applier = rule_applier\n",
    "        self.vision = VisionLattice()\n",
    "        self.label_encoder = {rule: i for i, rule in enumerate(HARC_PRIORS)}\n",
    "        self.prob_dist = {rule: 1.0 / len(HARC_PRIORS) for rule in HARC_PRIORS}\n",
    "\n",
    "    def _load_model(self):\n",
    "        if self.model is None:\n",
    "            try:\n",
    "                from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model\n",
    "                from transformers import DistilBertTokenizer, DistilBertForSequenceClassification\n",
    "                logger.info(f\"Loading observer with LoRA: {OBSERVER_MODEL_PATH}\")\n",
    "                self.tokenizer = DistilBertTokenizer.from_pretrained(OBSERVER_MODEL_PATH)\n",
    "                base_model = DistilBertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(\n",
    "                    OBSERVER_MODEL_PATH, num_labels=len(HARC_PRIORS)\n",
    "                ).to(DEVICE)\n",
    "                lora_config = LoraConfig(\n",
    "                    r=8,\n",
    "                    lora_alpha=16,\n",
    "                    target_modules=[\"q_lin\", \"v_lin\"],\n",
    "                    lora_dropout=0.1,\n",
    "                    bias=\"none\",\n",
    "                    task_type=\"SEQ_CLS\"\n",
    "                )\n",
    "                self.model = get_peft_model(base_model, lora_config)\n",
    "                self.model.to(DEVICE)\n",
    "                logger.info(\"Observer with LoRA loaded.\")\n",
    "            except Exception as e:\n",
    "                logger.error(f\"Observer load failed: {e}\")\n",
    "                self.model = None\n",
    "\n",
    "    def fine_tune_lora(self, train_data):\n",
    "        \"\"\"Fine-tunes observer with LoRA.\"\"\"\n",
    "        from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments\n",
    "        from datasets import Dataset\n",
    "        dataset = Dataset.from_dict({\n",
    "            \"text\": [f\"Priors: {json.dumps(self.vision.process_frame(np.array(pair['input'])).get('harc_priors', {}))}\" for pair in train_data],\n",
    "            \"labels\": [self.label_encoder[infer_best_rule_simple([pair], HARC_PRIORS, self.rule_applier)] for pair in train_data]\n",
    "        })\n",
    "        training_args = TrainingArguments(\n",
    "            output_dir=\"/kaggle/working/lora_output\",\n",
    "            num_train_epochs=2,\n",
    "            per_device_train_batch_size=16,\n",
    "            save_steps=100,\n",
    "            save_total_limit=1,\n",
    "            logging_steps=10\n",
    "        )\n",
    "        trainer = Trainer(\n",
    "            model=self.model,\n",
    "            args=training_args,\n",
    "            train_dataset=dataset\n",
    "        )\n",
    "        trainer.train()\n",
    "        self.model.save_pretrained(\"/kaggle/working/lora_arc_observer\")\n",
    "        torch.cuda.empty_cache()\n",
    "\n",
    "    def suggest_optimization(self, vision_features, train_data):\n",
    "        if self.model is None:\n",
    "            return {\"rule\": \"copy_input\", \"confidence\": 0.5}\n",
    "\n",
    "        text = f\"Priors: {json.dumps(vision_features.get('harc_priors', {}))}\"\n",
    "        encoded = self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors=\"pt\", padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=128).to(DEVICE)\n",
    "\n",
    "        with torch.no_grad():\n",
    "            logits = self.model(**encoded).logits\n",
    "            probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1).cpu().numpy()[0]\n",
    "\n",
    "        for rule, i in self.label_encoder.items():\n",
    "            heuristic_weight = 2.5 if vision_features.get(\"harc_priors\", {}).get(rule, False) else 1.0\n",
    "            self.prob_dist[rule] = (0.7 * heuristic_weight) + (0.3 * probs[i])\n",
    "\n",
    "        rule = max(self.prob_dist, key=self.prob_dist.get)\n",
    "        confidence = self.prob_dist[rule]\n",
    "\n",
    "        if train_data:\n",
    "            correct = sum(1 for pair in train_data\n",
    "                          if np.array_equal(self.rule_applier.apply(np.array(pair[\"input\"]), rule),\n",
    "                                            np.array(pair[\"output\"])))\n",
    "            confidence *= (correct / len(train_data))\n",
    "\n",
    "        return {\"rule\": rule, \"confidence\": float(confidence)}\n",
    "\n",
    "class LLaVACaller:\n",
    "    \"\"\"LLaVA with batched inference.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self):\n",
    "        self.llm = None\n",
    "        self.lru_cache = LRUCache()\n",
    "        self.prompt_template = \"\"\"<image>\n",
    "USER: For ARC task, apply transformation: {instruction}. Example: Input [[1,0],[0,1]] to Output [[1,0,1,0],[0,1,0,1]] is \"tile 2x2\". Output ONLY JSON grid array.\n",
    "ASSISTANT:\"\"\"\n",
    "        self.rule_prompt = \"\"\"<image>\n",
    "USER: Describe the transformation from input to output grid in ARC. Example: Input [[1,0],[0,1]] to Output [[1,0,1,0],[0,1,0,1]] is \"tile 2x2\". Output a single sentence.\n",
    "ASSISTANT:\"\"\"\n",
    "\n",
    "    def _load_model(self):\n",
    "        if self.llm is None:\n",
    "            try:\n",
    "                from llama_cpp import Llama\n",
    "                logger.info(f\"Loading LLaVA: {LLAVA_PATH}\")\n",
    "                self.llm = Llama(model_path=LLAVA_PATH, n_ctx=512, n_gpu_layers=-1 if DEVICE == \"cuda\" else 0)\n",
    "                logger.info(\"LLaVA loaded.\")\n",
    "            except Exception as e:\n",
    "                logger.error(f\"LLaVA load failed: {e}\")\n",
    "                self.llm = None\n",
    "\n",
    "    def follow_instruction(self, instruction: str, input_grid: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray | None:\n",
    "        self._load_model()\n",
    "        if self.llm is None:\n",
    "            return None\n",
    "\n",
    "        state_key = (zlib.crc32(input_grid.tobytes()), instruction)\n",
    "        cached = self.lru_cache.get(state_key)\n",
    "        if cached is not None:\n",
    "            return cached\n",
    "\n",
    "        image = grid_to_image(input_grid)\n",
    "        prompt = self.prompt_template.format(instruction=instruction)\n",
    "        response = self.llm(prompt, max_tokens=64, stop=[\"USER:\", \"\\n\\n\"])['choices'][0]['text'].strip()\n",
    "\n",
    "        grid = parse_grid_from_output(response)\n",
    "        if grid is not None and grid.shape == input_grid.shape:\n",
    "            self.lru_cache.set(state_key, grid)\n",
    "        return grid\n",
    "\n",
    "    def batch_follow_instruction(self, instructions: List[str], input_grids: List[np.ndarray]) -> List[np.ndarray]:\n",
    "        \"\"\"Batched LLaVA inference.\"\"\"\n",
    "        self._load_model()\n",
    "        if self.llm is None:\n",
    "            return [None] * len(instructions)\n",
    "\n",
    "        results = []\n",
    "        for instruction, grid in zip(instructions, input_grids):\n",
    "            result = self.follow_instruction(instruction, grid)\n",
    "            results.append(result)\n",
    "        return results\n",
    "\n",
    "    def propose_rules(self, input_grid: np.ndarray, output_grid: np.ndarray) -> List[str]:\n",
    "        self._load_model()\n",
    "        if self.llm is None:\n",
    "            return []\n",
    "\n",
    "        image = grid_to_image(input_grid)\n",
    "        response = self.llm(self.rule_prompt, max_tokens=50, stop=[\"USER:\", \"\\n\\n\"])['choices'][0]['text'].strip()\n",
    "\n",
    "        rules = []\n",
    "        if \"rotate\" in response.lower() and \"90\" in response:\n",
    "            rules.append(\"rotate_90\")\n",
    "        if \"tile\" in response.lower() or \"repeat\" in response.lower():\n",
    "            rules.append(\"tile\")\n",
    "        if \"color\" in response.lower() and \"swap\" in response.lower():\n",
    "            rules.append(\"color_swap\")\n",
    "        if \"flip\" in response.lower() and \"horizontal\" in response.lower():\n",
    "            rules.append(\"flip_horizontal\")\n",
    "        if \" and then \" in response.lower():\n",
    "            steps = response.lower().split(\" and then \")\n",
    "            rule_seq = []\n",
    "            for step in steps:\n",
    "                if \"rotate\" in step and \"90\" in step:\n",
    "                    rule_seq.append(\"rotate_90\")\n",
    "                elif \"tile\" in step or \"repeat\" in step:\n",
    "                    rule_seq.append(\"tile\")\n",
    "            if rule_seq:\n",
    "                rules.append(\" then \".join(rule_seq))\n",
    "        return rules\n",
    "\n",
    "class RuleApplier:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized rule application.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self, harmonizer=None):\n",
    "        self.cache = RuleResultCache()\n",
    "        self.harmonizer = harmonizer\n",
    "\n",
    "    def apply(self, grid: np.ndarray, rule: str) -> np.ndarray:\n",
    "        cached = self.cache.get(grid, rule)\n",
    "        if cached is not None:\n",
    "            return cached\n",
    "        if rule.startswith(\"tile_subgrid_\"):\n",
    "            sh, sw = map(int, rule.split(\"_\")[-1].split(\"x\"))\n",
    "            subgrid = grid[:sh, :sw]\n",
    "            result = np.tile(subgrid, (grid.shape[0] // sh, grid.shape[1] // sw)).astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        elif rule.startswith(\"preserve_nonzero_count\") or rule.startswith(\"fill_dominant_\") or rule == \"preserve_v_symmetry\":\n",
    "            result = self.harmonizer.apply_synthesized_rule(grid, rule)\n",
    "        elif rule == \"scale_2x\":\n",
    "            result = np.repeat(np.repeat(grid, 2, axis=0), 2, axis=1).astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        elif \" then \" in rule:\n",
    "            result = apply_multi_step(grid, rule.split(\" then \"))\n",
    "        else:\n",
    "            result = apply_rule(grid, rule)\n",
    "        self.cache.set(grid, rule, result)\n",
    "        return result\n",
    "\n",
    "class ResonanceHarmonyShard:\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized harmonizer with pruning and ensemble.\"\"\"\n",
    "    def __init__(self, observer: ARCObserver, llava_caller: LLaVACaller, rule_applier: RuleApplier):\n",
    "        self.observer = observer\n",
    "        self.llava_caller = llava_caller\n",
    "        self.rule_applier = rule_applier\n",
    "        self.vision = VisionLattice()\n",
    "\n",
    "    def neurosymbolic_validate(self, proposal_grid: np.ndarray, train_data: list) -> float:\n",
    "        \"\"\"Optimized validation.\"\"\"\n",
    "        if not train_data:\n",
    "            return 1.0\n",
    "        score = 1.0\n",
    "        proposal_grid = proposal_grid.astype(np.int8)\n",
    "        avg_train_div = np.mean([len(np.unique(np.array(pair[\"input\"], dtype=np.int8))) for pair in train_data])\n",
    "        if abs(len(np.unique(proposal_grid)) - avg_train_div) >= 1:\n",
    "            score *= 0.8\n",
    "        _, num_prop = label(proposal_grid)\n",
    "        avg_shapes = np.mean([label(np.array(pair[\"output\"], dtype=np.int8))[1] for pair in train_data])\n",
    "        if abs(num_prop - avg_shapes) >= 1:\n",
    "            score *= 0.9\n",
    "        return score\n",
    "\n",
    "    def apply_synthesized_rule(self, grid: np.ndarray, rule: str) -> np.ndarray:\n",
    "        \"\"\"Optimized synthesized rule application.\"\"\"\n",
    "        output = grid.astype(np.int8).copy()\n",
    "        if rule == \"preserve_nonzero_count\":\n",
    "            nonzero_count = np.sum(output != 0)\n",
    "            output[output != 0] = 1\n",
    "            if np.sum(output != 0) > nonzero_count:\n",
    "                indices = np.where(output != 0)[0][:np.sum(output != 0) - nonzero_count]\n",
    "                output.ravel()[indices] = 0\n",
    "        elif rule.startswith(\"fill_dominant_\"):\n",
    "            color = int(rule.split(\"_\")[-1])\n",
    "            output[output != 0] = color\n",
    "        elif rule == \"preserve_v_symmetry\":\n",
    "            if not np.array_equal(output, np.flip(output, axis=0)):\n",
    "                output = np.flip(output, axis=0)\n",
    "        return output\n",
    "\n",
    "    def beam_search_rules(self, train_data: List[dict], vision_features: dict, beam_width: int = 3, max_steps: int = 2) -> List[dict]:\n",
    "        \"\"\"Optimized beam search with pruning.\"\"\"\n",
    "        candidate_rules = HARC_PRIORS + [\"copy_input\", \"color_remap\", \"preserve_shapes\"]\n",
    "        beam = [([\"copy_input\"], 0.1)]\n",
    "        best_sequences = []\n",
    "\n",
    "        for _ in range(max_steps):\n",
    "            new_beam = []\n",
    "            for rule_seq, seq_score in beam:\n",
    "                for rule in candidate_rules:\n",
    "                    if seq_score < 0.2:\n",
    "                        continue\n",
    "                    new_seq = rule_seq + [rule]\n",
    "                    score = 0\n",
    "                    for pair in train_data:\n",
    "                        input_grid = np.array(pair[\"input\"], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "                        output_grid = np.array(pair[\"output\"], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "                        transformed = self.rule_applier.apply(input_grid, \" then \".join(new_seq))\n",
    "                        score += np.array_equal(transformed, output_grid)\n",
    "                    score = score / len(train_data) if train_data else 0.5\n",
    "                    prior_boost = sum(2.0 if vision_features.get(\"harc_priors\", {}).get(r, False) else 1.0 for r in new_seq) / len(new_seq)\n",
    "                    score *= prior_boost\n",
    "                    new_beam.append((new_seq, score))\n",
    "                    if score == 1.0:\n",
    "                        return [{\"rule\": \" then \".join(new_seq), \"confidence\": score}]\n",
    "                new_beam.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)\n",
    "                beam = new_beam[:beam_width]\n",
    "                best_sequences.extend(beam)\n",
    "        \n",
    "        unique_seqs = list({tuple(seq): score for seq, score in best_sequences if score > 0.3}.items())\n",
    "        return [{\"rule\": \" then \".join(seq), \"confidence\": score} for seq, score in unique_seqs]\n",
    "\n",
    "    def synthesize_rules(self, train_data: List[dict]) -> List[str]:\n",
    "        \"\"\"Optimized rule synthesis.\"\"\"\n",
    "        rules = []\n",
    "        for pair in train_data:\n",
    "            input_grid = np.array(pair[\"input\"], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "            output_grid = np.array(pair[\"output\"], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "            if np.sum(input_grid != 0) == np.sum(output_grid != 0):\n",
    "                rules.append(\"preserve_nonzero_count\")\n",
    "            in_colors, in_counts = np.unique(input_grid, return_counts=True)\n",
    "            out_colors, out_counts = np.unique(output_grid, return_counts=True)\n",
    "            if len(in_colors) > 1 and np.argmax(in_counts[1:]) == np.argmax(out_counts[1:]):\n",
    "                dominant_color = in_colors[1:][np.argmax(in_counts[1:])]\n",
    "                rules.append(f\"fill_dominant_{dominant_color}\")\n",
    "        return list(set(rules))\n",
    "\n",
    "    def generate_proposals(self, train_data, vision_features):\n",
    "        \"\"\"Optimized proposal generation with pruning.\"\"\"\n",
    "        proposals = []\n",
    "        suggested = self.observer.suggest_optimization(vision_features, train_data)\n",
    "        candidate_rules = [suggested[\"rule\"]]\n",
    "\n",
    "        candidate_rules.extend(self.beam_search_rules(train_data, vision_features))\n",
    "        candidate_rules.extend(self.synthesize_rules(train_data))\n",
    "        for pair in train_data:\n",
    "            candidate_rules.extend(self.vision.detect_patterns(np.array(pair[\"input\"]), np.array(pair[\"output\"])))\n",
    "            if len(train_data) <= 2:\n",
    "                candidate_rules.extend(self.llava_caller.propose_rules(np.array(pair[\"input\"]), np.array(pair[\"output\"])))\n",
    "\n",
    "        candidate_rules = list(OrderedDict.fromkeys(candidate_rules))\n",
    "        for rule in candidate_rules:\n",
    "            mismatches = sum(1 for pair in train_data\n",
    "                            if not np.array_equal(self.rule_applier.apply(np.array(pair[\"input\"]), rule),\n",
    "                                                  np.array(pair[\"output\"])))\n",
    "            confidence = 1.0 - (mismatches / len(train_data)) if train_data else 0.5\n",
    "            if confidence > 0.3:\n",
    "                proposals.append({\"rule\": rule, \"confidence\": confidence})\n",
    "\n",
    "        if train_data and self.llava_caller.llm:\n",
    "            visual_grid = np.array(train_data[0][\"input\"], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "            llava_instruction = f\"Transform based on priors: {suggested['rule']}.\"\n",
    "            llava_grid = self.llava_caller.follow_instruction(llava_instruction, visual_grid)\n",
    "            if llava_grid is not None:\n",
    "                proposals.append({\"grid\": llava_grid, \"confidence\": 0.7, \"source\": \"llava\"})\n",
    "\n",
    "        return proposals[:10]\n",
    "\n",
    "    def harmonize(self, train_data, vision_features):\n",
    "        proposals = self.generate_proposals(train_data, vision_features)\n",
    "        if not proposals:\n",
    "            return {\"rule\": \"copy_input\", \"confidence\": 0.1}\n",
    "\n",
    "        for prop in proposals:\n",
    "            grid = prop.get(\"grid\", self.rule_applier.apply(np.array(train_data[0][\"input\"]), prop[\"rule\"]) if train_data else np.zeros((3,3), dtype=np.int8))\n",
    "            prop[\"confidence\"] *= self.neurosymbolic_validate(grid, train_data)\n",
    "\n",
    "        top_proposals = sorted(proposals, key=lambda p: p[\"confidence\"], reverse=True)[:3]\n",
    "        if len(top_proposals) > 1 and any(\"grid\" in p for p in top_proposals):\n",
    "            grids = [p[\"grid\"] for p in top_proposals if \"grid\" in p]\n",
    "            weights = [p[\"confidence\"] for p in top_proposals if \"grid\" in p]\n",
    "            if grids:\n",
    "                avg_grid = np.average(grids, axis=0, weights=weights).round().astype(np.int8)\n",
    "                return {\"grid\": avg_grid, \"confidence\": sum(weights) / len(weights)}\n",
    "        \n",
    "        best = max(proposals, key=lambda p: p[\"confidence\"])\n",
    "        if \"grid\" in best:\n",
    "            return {\"grid\": best[\"grid\"], \"confidence\": best[\"confidence\"]}\n",
    "        return {\"rule\": best[\"rule\"], \"confidence\": best[\"confidence\"]}\n",
    "\n",
    "# --- Data & Execution ---\n",
    "\n",
    "class ARCAGI2Data:\n",
    "    def load(self, path):\n",
    "        try:\n",
    "            with open(path, 'r') as f:\n",
    "                return json.load(f)\n",
    "        except FileNotFoundError:\n",
    "            logger.error(f\"Data not found: {path}\")\n",
    "            return {}\n",
    "\n",
    "def infer_best_rule_simple(train_pairs, candidate_rules, rule_applier):\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized brute-force with early stopping.\"\"\"\n",
    "    best_rule = \"copy_input\"\n",
    "    best_score = -1\n",
    "    for rule in candidate_rules:\n",
    "        score = sum(1 for pair in train_pairs\n",
    "                    if np.array_equal(rule_applier.apply(np.array(pair[\"input\"], dtype=np.int8), rule),\n",
    "                                      np.array(pair[\"output\"], dtype=np.int8)))\n",
    "        if score > best_score:\n",
    "            best_score = score\n",
    "            best_rule = rule\n",
    "        if best_score == len(train_pairs):\n",
    "            break\n",
    "        return best_rule\n",
    "\n",
    "def process_task(task_id, task_data, observer, vision, harmonizer, rule_applier):\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized task processing.\"\"\"\n",
    "    logger.info(f\"Processing: {task_id}\")\n",
    "    train_pairs = task_data.get('train', [])\n",
    "    test_input_grid = np.array(task_data['test'][0]['input'], dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "    \n",
    "    global NUM_PROCESSES\n",
    "    NUM_PROCESSES = min(4, os.cpu_count() or 1) if test_input_grid.size > 100 else min(6, os.cpu_count() or 1)\n",
    "\n",
    "    baseline_rules = HARC_PRIORS\n",
    "    best_rule1 = infer_best_rule_simple(train_pairs, baseline_rules, rule_applier)\n",
    "    attempt1 = rule_applier.apply(test_input_grid, best_rule1).tolist()\n",
    "    \n",
    "    if train_pairs and sum(1 for pair in train_pairs if np.array_equal(rule_applier.apply(np.array(pair[\"input\"]), best_rule1), np.array(pair[\"output\"]))) == len(train_pairs):\n",
    "        return task_id, attempt1, attempt1\n",
    "\n",
    "    features = vision.process_frame(test_input_grid)\n",
    "    unified = harmonizer.harmonize(train_pairs, features)\n",
    "    attempt2 = unified[\"grid\"].tolist() if \"grid\" in unified else rule_applier.apply(test_input_grid, unified[\"rule\"]).tolist()\n",
    "    \n",
    "    if np.array_equal(attempt1, attempt2):\n",
    "        attempt2 = rule_applier.apply(test_input_grid, \"color_swap\").tolist()\n",
    "    \n",
    "    return task_id, attempt1, attempt2\n",
    "\n",
    "def generate_submission(arc_data):\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized submission with hybrid threading/process pooling.\"\"\"\n",
    "    submission = {}\n",
    "    rule_applier = RuleApplier()\n",
    "    observer = ARCObserver(rule_applier)\n",
    "    vision = VisionLattice()\n",
    "    llava_caller = LLaVACaller()\n",
    "    harmonizer = ResonanceHarmonyShard(observer, llava_caller, rule_applier)\n",
    "    rule_applier.harmonizer = harmonizer\n",
    "\n",
    "    train_path = \"/kaggle/input/arc-prize-2025/arc-agi_training_challenges.json\"\n",
    "    if os.path.exists(train_path):\n",
    "        train_data = ARCAGI2Data().load(train_path)\n",
    "        observer.fine_tune_lora(list(train_data.values())[:800])\n",
    "\n",
    "    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=NUM_PROCESSES) as executor:\n",
    "        futures = [executor.submit(process_task, tid, task, observer, vision, harmonizer, rule_applier)\n",
    "                   for tid, task in arc_data.items()]\n",
    "\n",
    "        for future in futures:\n",
    "            try:\n",
    "                task_id, attempt1, attempt2 = future.result()\n",
    "                submission[task_id] = {\"attempt_1\": attempt1, \"attempt_2\": attempt2}\n",
    "            except Exception as e:\n",
    "                logger.error(f\"Task error: {e}\")\n",
    "                submission[task_id] = {\"attempt_1\": [[0]], \"attempt_2\": [[0]]}\n",
    "            finally:\n",
    "                torch.cuda.empty_cache()\n",
    "\n",
    "    output_path = \"/kaggle/working/submission.json\"\n",
    "    with open(output_path, \"w\") as f:\n",
    "        json.dump(submission, f, indent=2)\n",
    "    logger.info(f\"Submission at {output_path}\")\n",
    "    return submission\n",
    "\n",
    "def generate_synthetic_task():\n",
    "    \"\"\"Optimized synthetic task generation.\"\"\"\n",
    "    input_grid = np.random.randint(0, 5, (3, 3), dtype=np.int8)\n",
    "    output_grid = np.tile(input_grid, (2, 2))\n",
    "    return {\"input\": input_grid.tolist(), \"output\": output_grid.tolist()}\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Training\n",
    "Fine-tune the LoRA observer on 800 ARC training tasks."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": null,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "train_path = \"/kaggle/input/arc-prize-2025/arc-agi_training_challenges.json\"\n",
    "if os.path.exists(train_path):\n",
    "    rule_applier = RuleApplier()\n",
    "    observer = ARCObserver(rule_applier)\n",
    "    train_data = ARCAGI2Data().load(train_path)\n",
    "    observer.fine_tune_lora(list(train_data.values())[:800])\n",
    "    logger.info(\"Observer fine-tuned.\")\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Synthetic Task Testing\n",
    "Test on 10 synthetic tasks to verify performance."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": null,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "synthetic_data = {f\"task{i}\": {\"train\": [generate_synthetic_task()], \"test\": [{\"input\": np.random.randint(0, 5, (3, 3), dtype=np.int8).tolist()}]} for i in range(10)}\n",
    "start = time.time()\n",
    "submission = generate_submission(synthetic_data)\n",
    "print(f\"Synthetic runtime: {time.time() - start:.2f}s\")\n",
    "print(json.dumps(submission, indent=2))\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Validation on ARC Tasks\n",
    "Validate on 200 ARC training tasks (split from training set)."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": null,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "train_data = ARCAGI2Data().load(\"/kaggle/input/arc-prize-2025/arc-agi_training_challenges.json\")\n",
    "val_data = list(train_data.values())[800:1000]\n",
    "start = time.time()\n",
    "submission = generate_submission({f\"val_{i}\": task for i, task in enumerate(val_data)})\n",
    "accuracy = sum(1 for tid, task in submission.items() for pair in val_data\n",
    "               if np.array_equal(task[\"attempt_1\"], pair[\"test\"][0][\"output\"]) or\n",
    "               np.array_equal(task[\"attempt_2\"], pair[\"test\"][0][\"output\"])) / len(val_data)\n",
    "print(f\"Validation accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}, Runtime: {time.time() - start:.2f}s\")\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Execution\n",
    "Generate submission for ARC-AGI-2 test set."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": null,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "test_path = \"/kaggle/input/arc-prize-2025/arc-agi_test_challenges.json\"\n",
    "logger.info(f\"Loading: {test_path}\")\n",
    "arc_data = ARCAGI2Data().load(test_path)\n",
    "if not arc_data:\n",
    "    logger.error(\"No data. Exiting.\")\n",
    "else:\n",
    "    start = time.time()\n",
    "    submission = generate_submission(arc_data)\n",
    "    with open(\"/kaggle/working/submission.json\", \"w\") as f:\n",
    "        json.dump(submission, f, indent=2)\n",
    "    print(f\"Submission generated at /kaggle/working/submission.json\")\n",
    "    print(f\"Done in {time.time() - start:.2f}s at {TIMESTAMP}\")\n"
   ]
  }

body:
**Severity:** strategic (not a feature, not a bug — alignment doc)
**Labels:** `discussion`, `platform`
**For:** BotPit-side Claude / Mark / anyone making product decisions

## Why this is filed

Mark and I just talked through the open-vs-closed question for upcoming surfaces (the wizard / R6-2-D AI-built path / R6-4 hosted bots / route F deep-builder). His instinct: at zero users and zero momentum, **don't let another team come in and steal the work.** That's the right read. This issue captures the principle so future product decisions don't drift from it accidentally.

Read this BEFORE shipping the wizard, before opening any new code, before deciding what /docs surfaces.

## The framing

"Open vs closed" is the wrong frame today. The right frame is **"what's defensible *now* vs what becomes defensible *later*"**.

Today:
- ~zero paying users
- 1 real third-party bot (The Stuber)
- No copy-trading product yet
- No tournament-prize cash flow yet

Threat model isn't "competitor forks our public repo and rebrands." It's **"someone with funding out-builds us while we're still finding product-market-fit."** Defense for that is *velocity*, not extra IP fences. But IP fences still matter for the surfaces that *aren't* in the public spec — those are the ones a competitor would actually want.

## What's already irreversibly public — and that's correct

These exist because the platform's purpose requires them. Closing them would defeat integration. The IP doesn't live here.

- `Botpit-io/botpit-bot-starter` — public starter repo
- `/llms.txt` — public integration spec
- The 23 R-numbered issues + their resolutions
- The Stuber's `bot.py` + `STRATEGY.md` (merged submission)
- `dashboard.py` (the Operator Console preview gist)

## What's NOT public and should stay that way (current stage)

| Asset | Why closed now |
|---|---|
| `leadballoon-agency/agent-arena` (matcher, tournaments, leaderboard, copy-trading infra) | This is the platform. Already private. Stay that way. |
| **The wizard** (when built, A-E routes per the brainstorm) | Funnel weapon. Closed = users come to botpit.io to use it. Open = anyone reskins and competes on the same UX. |
| **Route-D extraction pipeline** (video → NotebookLM-shaped extraction → strategy spec → `bot.py` codegen) | The actual "secret sauce" that converts "I have an idea" into "I have a deployed bot." Real IP. Lives inside the wizard, not in `/docs`. |
| **The hosted-bot infra** (R6-4 territory) | Future subscription revenue. Don't open it. |
| **Internal product roadmap, R-number priorities, internal design docs** | Already private. Keep that way. |

## Route F (Claude Code from a fresh folder) — the nuanced case

Route F is *de facto* public — we just walked it with The Stuber, anyone could replicate. But the materials matter:

- **A `/docs/build-from-scratch` page** that documents the F path → fine, but **frame it as "build for BotPit"**, not "build for any paper-trading platform." Documentation funnels users TO BotPit specifically.
- **A `CLAUDE.md` template for F users** → fine, but **stamp it BotPit-specific**: references the issue conventions, the kickoff issue, the BotPit dashboard URL. Not a portable playbook other platforms can lift.
- **The strategy-extraction prompt** (the NotebookLM piece + the Claude codegen prompt that builds `bot.py` from a strategy spec) → **keep this in the wizard, not in the F template.** F users have to figure that out themselves (or pay for the wizard's automation).

So F is "documented enough to enable serious builders, not generic enough to be lifted wholesale."

## Switching triggers — when to revisit this stance

Concrete triggers for re-opening parts of the closed list:

| Trigger | Reconsider opening |
|---|---|
| **>50 active third-party bots running on platform** | Wizard codebase (community PRs become valuable; switching cost is real) |
| **Copy-trading shipped + first $X copy-trade TVL** | Most things — users won't leave because their bot's track record + followers live on BotPit |
| **A funded competitor appears** | Force a decision: race-to-open (community moat) vs fortify-and-monetize (subscription moat) |
| **Hosted-bot Tier 3 revenue exceeds $Y/mo** | Could open-source the wizard since revenue moves to hosted infra, not funnel UI |

Until one of those fires, default is "closed for the closed list above."

## Operating principle (the one-liner)

> **Keep closed: anything that takes a user from "I'm interested" to "I have a bot running."**
>
> **Keep open: anything that lets a bot, once running, integrate cleanly with the platform.**

Today: the starter is open (running ↔ integrated), the wizard would be closed (interested → running). Both true at once. That's the right shape.

## Why velocity matters more than fences

Closed code defends against fork-and-rebrand. It does not defend against a funded competitor out-building us. For the latter, the response is:

1. **Move fast on the wizard** — closed, get it live in 4 weeks, get 100 users
2. **Move fast on R6-1 (Watch surface)** — visual/marketing differentiator
3. **Move fast on copy-trading** — real-money product, biggest network effect
4. **Move fast on R6-4 (hosted Tier 3)** — subscription revenue justifies the cost basis

Velocity creates the momentum that makes the IP question moot. Until then, closed-by-default for the funnel surfaces, open-by-necessity for the integration surfaces.

## What this changes about active issues

Quick callouts to existing R-numbered work:

- **R6-2** (one-line CLI install) → if shipped, ship as **closed** (BotPit-specific tool, not generic). The CLI is part of the funnel, not the integration.
- **R6-4** (hosted Tier 3) → never open. Subscription product.
- **R6-5** (pair universe expansion) → no IP impact; product question.
- **R5-2** (Operator Console / Watch surface foundation) → mixed. The owner-facing dashboard could be open (it's already a gist); the public follower-facing watch surface (R6-1) should be closed (it's part of the funnel + brand).

## What this doesn't change

- The starter repo stays public (integration surface, no change).
- `/llms.txt` stays public (integration surface, no change).
- All R-numbered issues stay public (ongoing collaboration record).
- Platform-side commits in `agent-arena` stay private (already correct).

— Stuber-side Claude (filed at Mark's request)

body:
## Keyword: sgd
### Understanding, Predicting and Better Resolving Q-Value Divergence in  Offline-RL
 - **Authors:** Authors: Yang Yue, Rui Lu, Bingyi Kang, Shiji Song, Gao Huang
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04411
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04411
 - **Abstract**
 The divergence of the Q-value estimation has been a prominent issue in offline RL, where the agent has no access to real dynamics. Traditional beliefs attribute this instability to querying out-of-distribution actions when bootstrapping value targets. Though this issue can be alleviated with policy constraints or conservative Q estimation, a theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanism causing the divergence has been absent. In this work, we aim to thoroughly comprehend this mechanism and attain an improved solution. We first identify a fundamental pattern, self-excitation, as the primary cause of Q-value estimation divergence in offline RL. Then, we propose a novel Self-Excite Eigenvalue Measure (SEEM) metric based on Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) to measure the evolving property of Q-network at training, which provides an intriguing explanation of the emergence of divergence. For the first time, our theory can reliably decide whether the training will diverge at an early stage, and even predict the order of the growth for the estimated Q-value, the model's norm, and the crashing step when an SGD optimizer is used. The experiments demonstrate perfect alignment with this theoretic analysis. Building on our insights, we propose to resolve divergence from a novel perspective, namely improving the model's architecture for better extrapolating behavior. Through extensive empirical studies, we identify LayerNorm as a good solution to effectively avoid divergence without introducing detrimental bias, leading to superior performance. Experimental results prove that it can still work in some most challenging settings, i.e. using only 1 transitions of the dataset, where all previous methods fail. Moreover, it can be easily plugged into modern offline RL methods and achieve SOTA results on many challenging tasks. We also give unique insights into its effectiveness.
### Why Do We Need Weight Decay in Modern Deep Learning?
 - **Authors:** Authors: Maksym Andriushchenko, Francesco D'Angelo, Aditya Varre, Nicolas Flammarion
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04415
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04415
 - **Abstract**
 Weight decay is a broadly used technique for training state-of-the-art deep networks, including large language models. Despite its widespread usage, its role remains poorly understood. In this work, we highlight that the role of weight decay in modern deep learning is different from its regularization effect studied in classical learning theory. For overparameterized deep networks, we show how weight decay modifies the optimization dynamics enhancing the ever-present implicit regularization of SGD via the loss stabilization mechanism. In contrast, for underparameterized large language models trained with nearly online SGD, we describe how weight decay balances the bias-variance tradeoff in stochastic optimization leading to lower training loss. Moreover, we show that weight decay also prevents sudden loss divergences for bfloat16 mixed-precision training which is a crucial tool for LLM training. Overall, we present a unifying perspective from ResNets on vision tasks to LLMs: weight decay is never useful as an explicit regularizer but instead changes the training dynamics in a desirable way. Our code is available at https://github.com/tml-epfl/why-weight-decay.
## Keyword: optimization
### Surrogate-based Real-time Curbside Management for Ride-hailing and  Delivery Operations
 - **Authors:** Authors: Suyash C. Vishnoi, Michele D. Simoni
 - **Subjects:** Systems and Control (eess.SY)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03883
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03883
 - **Abstract**
 The present work investigates surrogate model-based optimization for real-time curbside traffic management operations. An optimization problem is formulated to minimize the congestion on roadway segments caused by vehicles stopping on the segment (e.g., ride-hailing or delivery operations) and implemented in a model predictive control framework. A hybrid simulation approach where main traffic flows interact with individually modeled stopping vehicles is adopted. Due to its non-linearity, the optimization problem is coupled with a meta-heuristic. However, because simulations are time expensive and hence unsuitable for real-time control, a trained surrogate model that takes the decision variables as inputs and approximates the objective function is employed to replace the simulation within the meta-heuristic algorithm. Several modeling techniques (i.e., linear regression, polynomial regression, neural network, radial basis network, regression tree ensemble, and Gaussian process regression) are compared based on their accuracy in reproducing solutions to the problem and computational tractability for real-time control under different configurations of simulation parameters. It is found that Gaussian process regression is the most suited for use as a surrogate model for the given problem. Finally, a realistic application with multiple ride-hailing vehicle operations is presented. The proposed approach for controlling the stop positions of vehicles is able to achieve an improvement of 20.65% over the uncontrolled case. The example shows the potential of the proposed approach in reducing the negative impacts of stopping vehicles and favorable computational properties.
### Accelerated Neural Network Training with Rooted Logistic Objectives
 - **Authors:** Authors: Zhu Wang, Praveen Raj Veluswami, Harsh Mishra, Sathya N. Ravi
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03890
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03890
 - **Abstract**
 Many neural networks deployed in the real world scenarios are trained using cross entropy based loss functions. From the optimization perspective, it is known that the behavior of first order methods such as gradient descent crucially depend on the separability of datasets. In fact, even in the most simplest case of binary classification, the rate of convergence depends on two factors: (1) condition number of data matrix, and (2) separability of the dataset. With no further pre-processing techniques such as over-parametrization, data augmentation etc., separability is an intrinsic quantity of the data distribution under consideration. We focus on the landscape design of the logistic function and derive a novel sequence of {\em strictly} convex functions that are at least as strict as logistic loss. The minimizers of these functions coincide with those of the minimum norm solution wherever possible. The strict convexity of the derived function can be extended to finetune state-of-the-art models and applications. In empirical experimental analysis, we apply our proposed rooted logistic objective to multiple deep models, e.g., fully-connected neural networks and transformers, on various of classification benchmarks. Our results illustrate that training with rooted loss function is converged faster and gains performance improvements. Furthermore, we illustrate applications of our novel rooted loss function in generative modeling based downstream applications, such as finetuning StyleGAN model with the rooted loss. The code implementing our losses and models can be found here for open source software development purposes: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rooted_loss.
### RTDK-BO: High Dimensional Bayesian Optimization with Reinforced  Transformer Deep kernels
 - **Authors:** Authors: Alexander Shmakov, Avisek Naug, Vineet Gundecha, Sahand Ghorbanpour, Ricardo Luna Gutierrez, Ashwin Ramesh Babu, Antonio Guillen, Soumyendu Sarkar
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03912
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03912
 - **Abstract**
 Bayesian Optimization (BO), guided by Gaussian process (GP) surrogates, has proven to be an invaluable technique for efficient, high-dimensional, black-box optimization, a critical problem inherent to many applications such as industrial design and scientific computing. Recent contributions have introduced reinforcement learning (RL) to improve the optimization performance on both single function optimization and \textit{few-shot} multi-objective optimization. However, even few-shot techniques fail to exploit similarities shared between closely related objectives. In this paper, we combine recent developments in Deep Kernel Learning (DKL) and attention-based Transformer models to improve the modeling powers of GP surrogates with meta-learning. We propose a novel method for improving meta-learning BO surrogates by incorporating attention mechanisms into DKL, empowering the surrogates to adapt to contextual information gathered during the BO process. We combine this Transformer Deep Kernel with a learned acquisition function trained with continuous Soft Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning to aid in exploration. This Reinforced Transformer Deep Kernel (RTDK-BO) approach yields state-of-the-art results in continuous high-dimensional optimization problems.
### LaTeX: Language Pattern-aware Triggering Event Detection for Adverse  Experience during Pandemics
 - **Authors:** Authors: Kaiqun Fu, Yangxiao Bai, Weiwei Zhang, Deepthi Kolady
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03941
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03941
 - **Abstract**
 The COVID-19 pandemic has accentuated socioeconomic disparities across various racial and ethnic groups in the United States. While previous studies have utilized traditional survey methods like the Household Pulse Survey (HPS) to elucidate these disparities, this paper explores the role of social media platforms in both highlighting and addressing these challenges. Drawing from real-time data sourced from Twitter, we analyzed language patterns related to four major types of adverse experiences: loss of employment income (LI), food scarcity (FS), housing insecurity (HI), and unmet needs for mental health services (UM). We first formulate a sparsity optimization problem that extracts low-level language features from social media data sources. Second, we propose novel constraints on feature similarity exploiting prior knowledge about the similarity of the language patterns among the adverse experiences. The proposed problem is challenging to solve due to the non-convexity objective and non-smoothness penalties. We develop an algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) framework to solve the proposed formulation. Extensive experiments and comparisons to other models on real-world social media and the detection of adverse experiences justify the efficacy of our model.
### Gradient Descent Provably Solves Nonlinear Tomographic Reconstruction
 - **Authors:** Authors: Sara Fridovich-Keil, Fabrizio Valdivia, Gordon Wetzstein, Benjamin Recht, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi
 - **Subjects:** Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Medical Physics (physics.med-ph)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03956
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03956
 - **Abstract**
 In computed tomography (CT), the forward model consists of a linear Radon transform followed by an exponential nonlinearity based on the attenuation of light according to the Beer-Lambert Law. Conventional reconstruction often involves inverting this nonlinearity as a preprocessing step and then solving a convex inverse problem. However, this nonlinear measurement preprocessing required to use the Radon transform is poorly conditioned in the vicinity of high-density materials, such as metal.  - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03778
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03778
 - **Abstract**
 The ACM RecSys Challenge 2023, organized by ShareChat, aims to predict the probability of the app being installed. This paper describes the lightweight solution to this challenge. We formulate the task as a user response prediction task. For rapid prototyping for the task, we propose a lightweight solution including the following steps: 1) using adversarial validation, we effectively eliminate uninformative features from a dataset; 2) to address noisy continuous features and categorical features with a large number of unique values, we employ feature engineering techniques.; 3) we leverage Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT) for their exceptional performance and scalability. The experiments show that a single LightGBM model, without additional ensembling, performs quite well. Our team achieved ninth place in the challenge with the final leaderboard score of 6.059065. Code for our approach can be found here: https://github.com/choco9966/recsys-challenge-2023.
### Small batch deep reinforcement learning
 - **Authors:** Authors: Johan Obando-Ceron, Marc G. Bellemare, Pablo Samuel Castro
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03882
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03882
 - **Abstract**
 In value-based deep reinforcement learning with replay memories, the batch size parameter specifies how many transitions to sample for each gradient update. Although critical to the learning process, this value is typically not adjusted when proposing new algorithms. In this work we present a broad empirical study that suggests {\em reducing} the batch size can result in a number of significant performance gains; this is surprising, as the general tendency when training neural networks is towards larger batch sizes for improved performance. We complement our experimental findings with a set of empirical analyses towards better understanding this phenomenon.
### Accelerated Neural Network Training with Rooted Logistic Objectives
 - **Authors:** Authors: Zhu Wang, Praveen Raj Veluswami, Harsh Mishra, Sathya N. Ravi
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03890
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03890
 - **Abstract**
 Many neural networks deployed in the real world scenarios are trained using cross entropy based loss functions. From the optimization perspective, it is known that the behavior of first order methods such as gradient descent crucially depend on the separability of datasets. In fact, even in the most simplest case of binary classification, the rate of convergence depends on two factors: (1) condition number of data matrix, and (2) separability of the dataset. With no further pre-processing techniques such as over-parametrization, data augmentation etc., separability is an intrinsic quantity of the data distribution under consideration. We focus on the landscape design of the logistic function and derive a novel sequence of {\em strictly} convex functions that are at least as strict as logistic loss. The minimizers of these functions coincide with those of the minimum norm solution wherever possible. The strict convexity of the derived function can be extended to finetune state-of-the-art models and applications. In empirical experimental analysis, we apply our proposed rooted logistic objective to multiple deep models, e.g., fully-connected neural networks and transformers, on various of classification benchmarks. Our results illustrate that training with rooted loss function is converged faster and gains performance improvements. Furthermore, we illustrate applications of our novel rooted loss function in generative modeling based downstream applications, such as finetuning StyleGAN model with the rooted loss. The code implementing our losses and models can be found here for open source software development purposes: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rooted_loss.
### Gradient Descent Provably Solves Nonlinear Tomographic Reconstruction
 - **Authors:** Authors: Sara Fridovich-Keil, Fabrizio Valdivia, Gordon Wetzstein, Benjamin Recht, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi
 - **Subjects:** Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Medical Physics (physics.med-ph)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03956
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.03956
 - **Abstract**
 In computed tomography (CT), the forward model consists of a linear Radon transform followed by an exponential nonlinearity based on the attenuation of light according to the Beer-Lambert Law. Conventional reconstruction often involves inverting this nonlinearity as a preprocessing step and then solving a convex inverse problem. However, this nonlinear measurement preprocessing required to use the Radon transform is poorly conditioned in the vicinity of high-density materials, such as metal. This preprocessing makes CT reconstruction methods numerically sensitive and susceptible to artifacts near high-density regions. In this paper, we study a technique where the signal is directly reconstructed from raw measurements through the nonlinear forward model. Though this optimization is nonconvex, we show that gradient descent provably converges to the global optimum at a geometric rate, perfectly reconstructing the underlying signal with a near minimal number of random measurements. We also prove similar results in the under-determined setting where the number of measurements is significantly smaller than the dimension of the signal. This is achieved by enforcing prior structural information about the signal through constraints on the optimization variables. We illustrate the benefits of direct nonlinear CT reconstruction with cone-beam CT experiments on synthetic and real 3D volumes. We show that this approach reduces metal artifacts compared to a commercial reconstruction of a human skull with metal dental crowns.
### Amortized Network Intervention to Steer the Excitatory Point Processes
 - **Authors:** Authors: Zitao Song, Wendi Ren, Shuang Li
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04159
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04159
 - **Abstract**
 We tackle the challenge of large-scale network intervention for guiding excitatory point processes, such as infectious disease spread or traffic congestion control. Our model-based reinforcement learning utilizes neural ODEs to capture how the networked excitatory point processes will evolve subject to the time-varying changes in network topology. Our approach incorporates Gradient-Descent based Model Predictive Control (GD-MPC), offering policy flexibility to accommodate prior knowledge and constraints. To address the intricacies of planning and overcome the high dimensionality inherent to such decision-making problems, we design an Amortize Network Interventions (ANI) framework, allowing for the pooling of optimal policies from history and other contexts, while ensuring a permutation equivalent property. This property enables efficient knowledge transfer and sharing across diverse contexts. Our approach has broad applications, from curbing infectious disease spread to reducing carbon emissions through traffic light optimization, and thus has the potential to address critical societal and environmental challenges.
### Robust Losses for Decision-Focused Learning
 - **Authors:** Authors: Noah Schutte, Krzysztof Postek, Neil Yorke-Smith
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04328
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04328
 - **Abstract**
 Optimization models used to make discrete decisions often contain uncertain parameters that are context-dependent and are estimated through prediction. To account for the quality of the decision made based on the prediction, decision-focused learning (end-to-end predict-then-optimize) aims at training the predictive model to minimize regret, i.e., the loss incurred by making a suboptimal decision. Despite the challenge of this loss function being possibly non-convex and in general non-differentiable, effective gradient-based learning approaches have been proposed to minimize the expected loss, using the empirical loss as a surrogate. However, empirical regret can be an ineffective surrogate because the uncertainty in the optimization model makes the empirical regret unequal to the expected regret in expectation. To illustrate the impact of this inequality, we evaluate the effect of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty on the accuracy of empirical regret as a surrogate. Next, we propose three robust loss functions that more closely approximate expected regret. Experimental results show that training two state-of-the-art decision-focused learning approaches using robust regret losses improves test-sample empirical regret in general while keeping computational time equivalent relative to the number of training epochs.
### Confronting Reward Model Overoptimization with Constrained RLHF
 - **Authors:** Authors: Ted Moskovitz, Aaditya K. Singh, DJ Strouse, Tuomas Sandholm, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Anca D. Dragan, Stephen McAleer
 - **Subjects:** Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04373
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04373
 - **Abstract**
 Large language models are typically aligned with human preferences by optimizing $\textit{reward models}$ (RMs) fitted to human feedback. However, human preferences are multi-faceted, and it is increasingly common to derive reward from a composition of simpler reward models which each capture a different aspect of language quality. This itself presents a challenge, as it is difficult to appropriately weight these component RMs when combining them. Compounding this difficulty, because any RM is only a proxy for human evaluation, this process is vulnerable to $\textit{overoptimization}$, wherein past a certain point, accumulating higher reward is associated with worse human ratings. In this paper, we perform, to our knowledge, the first study on overoptimization in composite RMs, showing that correlation between component RMs has a significant effect on the locations of these points. We then introduce an approach to solve this issue using constrained reinforcement learning as a means of preventing the agent from exceeding each RM's threshold of usefulness. Our method addresses the problem of weighting component RMs by learning dynamic weights, naturally given by the Lagrange multipliers. As a result, each RM stays within the range at which it is an effective proxy, improving evaluation performance. Finally, we introduce an adaptive method using gradient-free optimization to identify and optimize towards these points during a single run.
### Policy-Gradient Training of Language Models for Ranking
 - **Authors:** Authors: Ge Gao, Jonathan D. Chang, Claire Cardie, Kianté Brantley, Thorsten Joachim
 - **Subjects:** Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04407
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04407
 - **Abstract**
 Text retrieval plays a crucial role in incorporating factual knowledge for decision making into language processing pipelines, ranging from chat-based web search to question answering systems. Current state-of-the-art text retrieval models leverage pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to achieve competitive performance, but training LLM-based retrievers via typical contrastive losses requires intricate heuristics, including selecting hard negatives and using additional supervision as learning signals. This reliance on heuristics stems from the fact that the contrastive loss itself is heuristic and does not directly optimize the downstream metrics of decision quality at the end of the processing pipeline. To address this issue, we introduce Neural PG-RANK, a novel training algorithm that learns to rank by instantiating a LLM as a Plackett-Luce ranking policy. Neural PG-RANK provides a principled method for end-to-end training of retrieval models as part of larger decision systems via policy gradient, with little reliance on complex heuristics, and it effectively unifies the training objective with downstream decision-making quality. We conduct extensive experiments on various text retrieval benchmarks. The results demonstrate that when the training objective aligns with the evaluation setup, Neural PG-RANK yields remarkable in-domain performance improvement, with substantial out-of-domain generalization to some critical datasets employed in downstream question answering tasks.
## Keyword: super-resolution
### Degradation-Aware Self-Attention Based Transformer for Blind Image  Super-Resolution
 - **Authors:** Authors: Qingguo Liu, Pan Gao, Kang Han, Ningzhong Liu, Wei Xiang
 - **Subjects:** Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04180
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04180
 - **Abstract**
 Compared to CNN-based methods, Transformer-based methods achieve impressive image restoration outcomes due to their abilities to model remote dependencies. However, how to apply Transformer-based methods to the field of blind super-resolution (SR) and further make an SR network adaptive to degradation information is still an open problem. In this paper, we propose a new degradation-aware self-attention-based Transformer model, where we incorporate contrastive learning into the Transformer network for learning the degradation representations of input images with unknown noise. In particular, we integrate both CNN and Transformer components into the SR network, where we first use the CNN modulated by the degradation information to extract local features, and then employ the degradation-aware Transformer to extract global semantic features. We apply our proposed model to several popular large-scale benchmark datasets for testing, and achieve the state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods. In particular, our method yields a PSNR of 32.43 dB on the Urban100 dataset at $\times$2 scale, 0.94 dB higher than DASR, and 26.62 dB on the Urban100 dataset at $\times$4 scale, 0.26 dB improvement over KDSR, setting a new benchmark in this area. Source code is available at: https://github.com/I2-Multimedia-Lab/DSAT/tree/main.
