---

## 9. Funding: Can We Get It? How? How Hard Is It?

### Will We Get Funding At All?

**Short answer: Yes, very likely.** Here's why:

| Factor | In Our Favor? | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **Market timing** | :white_check_mark: YES | AI agent infra is THE hottest VC category in 2025-2026 |
| **Differentiated positioning** | :white_check_mark: YES | "F1 for AI agents" — no one else does this. VCs love category creators |
| **Validated demand** | :white_check_mark: YES | Chatbot Arena proved the "arena" concept; SWE-bench proved agent eval demand |
| **Adjacent funding proof** | :white_check_mark: YES | $500M+ deployed into adjacent companies (LangSmith, Braintrust, Arize, W&B) |
| **Open-source advantage** | :white_check_mark: YES | OSS + cloud is the playbook VCs love (GitLab, Supabase, PostHog model) |
| **Technical moat** | :white_check_mark: YES | Replay corpus, challenge packs, sandboxed execution — not trivially replicable |
| **Revenue before raise** | :grey_question: PARTIAL | Pre-revenue is fine for seed, but even $5-10K MRR makes the story much stronger |
| **Team** | :grey_question: DEPENDS | VCs fund teams first. Technical depth + domain expertise matters |
| **Traction metrics** | :grey_question: BUILD THESE | GitHub stars, waitlist size, design partner commitments |

**Comparable raises that prove this is fundable:**

| Company | Stage | Amount | What They Had | Year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Confident AI (DeepEval) | Seed | $4M | OSS eval framework, YC batch | 2024 |
| AgentOps | Seed | ~$3M | Agent observability, early product | 2024 |
| Parea AI | Seed | ~$2M | Prompt eval tool, YC batch | 2023 |
| Braintrust | Seed | $5.1M | Eval framework, early design partners | 2023 |
| LangChain | Seed | $10M | OSS framework, massive GitHub traction | 2023 |

**AgentClash has a more differentiated product thesis than most of these at their seed stage.**

### How Difficult Is It?

**Difficulty level: MODERATE** — achievable but requires focused effort.

#### The Honest Breakdown

| Aspect | Difficulty | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Getting meetings** | EASY | AI infra is hot. VCs are actively looking. Cold emails work if the pitch is sharp |
| **Telling the story** | EASY | "F1 for AI agents" is a one-line pitch that clicks immediately |
| **Showing the product** | MODERATE | Need a compelling demo: run a live race, show the replay, show the leaderboard |
| **Proving demand** | MODERATE | Need 3-5 design partners or LOIs. Even verbal commitments from AI team leads help |
| **Proving team** | VARIES | Technical founder(s) who can ship fast. If solo, it's harder — VCs want 2-3 co-founders |
| **Competing for attention** | HARD | Every AI startup is fundraising. Need to stand out. The arena concept helps |
| **Negotiating terms** | MODERATE | Seed terms are fairly standard. Don't optimize for valuation — optimize for the right partner |

#### Realistic Timeline

```
Week 1-2:   Polish deck, record demo, build target VC list (50-80 firms)
Week 3-4:   Warm intros + cold outreach. Aim for 20-30 first meetings
Week 5-8:   Partner meetings, deep dives, reference checks
Week 9-12:  Term sheets, negotiation, close
```

**Total: 2-3 months** if you're focused. Can stretch to 4-6 months if you're building product simultaneously.

### How to Get Funding: The Playbook

#### Step 1: Build Fundable Traction (Before You Pitch)

These are the metrics VCs will ask about. Build them BEFORE the first meeting:

| Metric | Target Before Raise | How to Get There |
|---|---|---|
| **GitHub stars** | 500-1,000+ | HN launch, Reddit posts, AI Twitter, ProductHunt |
| **Waitlist** | 500-2,000 emails | Landing page + content marketing + social |
| **Design partners** | 3-5 signed LOIs | Cold outreach to AI team leads at known agent-building companies |
| **Demo** | Live race, replay, leaderboard | Build and polish the core UX flow |
| **OSS contributors** | 5-10 external contributors | Good first issues, community engagement |
| **Content / brand** | 3-5 benchmark reports published | Race popular models, publish results on blog + Twitter |

#### Step 2: Target the Right Investors

**Tier 1 — Best fit for AgentClash (AI infra focused):**
- **a16z** (invested in Braintrust, LangChain — they know this space intimately)
- **Sequoia** (invested in LangChain — looking for the next layer)
- **Lightspeed** (invested in Patronus AI — active in eval space)
- **Amplify Partners** (invested in Weights & Biases early)
- **Battery Ventures** (invested in Galileo AI)
- **Felicis Ventures** (active in AI infra)
- **Madrona** (active in AI developer tools)

**Tier 2 — Strong AI generalists:**
- **Greylock**
- **Index Ventures**
- **Accel**
- **Benchmark**
- **Founders Fund**

**Tier 3 — Accelerators (if pre-product-market-fit):**
- **Y Combinator** — best brand signal, $500K + $375K MFN SAFE
- **Neo** — strong for technical founders
- **Antler** — active globally
- **Techstars** — wide network

**Tier 4 — Angels who amplify:**
- AI company founders/execs who can be design partners AND investors
- DevTools founders who've been through this
- Model company DevRel leads who want independent benchmarks to exist

#### Step 3: The Pitch Narrative

**The deck structure that works for this:**

1. **Problem**: Teams don't know which agent to deploy. Current eval tools measure LLM calls, not agents. Benchmarks are academic, stale, and gameable.
2. **Insight**: "Same model, different agent" — evaluation should be at the system level, not the model level. And it should be competitive, not isolated.
3. **Product**: AgentClash — head-to-head agent races on real tasks. Live scoring on correctness, cost, latency, reliability. Full replay to see WHY.
4. **Demo**: Live race. Two agents. Same task. Watch them go. Show the replay. Show the scorecard.
5. **Market**: $47B AI agent market, 40% CAGR. $2-4B SAM for eval/observability. Category is forming NOW.
6. **Traction**: Stars, waitlist, design partners, benchmark reports published.
7. **Business model**: Free arena (growth) + paid workspace (revenue). $149-$999/mo.
8. **Competition**: Show the positioning map. We're the only ones in the agent-level + benchmark-first quadrant.
9. **Team**: Why we're the ones to build this. Technical depth + domain knowledge.
10. **Ask**: $2-4M seed to get to $500K ARR in 12 months.

#### Step 4: The Ask

| Stage | Typical Range | What You Trade | What You Get |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pre-seed** | $500K-$1.5M | 10-15% equity | Runway to build MVP + get design partners |
| **Seed** | $2M-$5M | 15-20% equity | Runway to launch, hire 3-5 people, get to $300K+ ARR |
| **Series A** | $8M-$20M | 15-25% equity | Scale team to 15-25, push to $1M+ ARR |

**Recommended: Raise a $2-4M seed round.** This gives 18-24 months of runway to:
- Hire 2-3 engineers
- Launch the cloud platform
- Get to 50+ paying workspaces
- Build the public arena
- Hit $300K-$500K ARR (Series A territory)

### What Could Go Wrong (Funding Risks)

| Risk | How It Kills Funding | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Solo founder** | VCs strongly prefer 2-3 co-founders | Find a co-founder OR show you can ship fast alone + have advisors |
| **No traction** | "Cool idea but come back when you have users" | Build traction BEFORE pitching. GitHub stars + design partners |
| **Market timing doubt** | "Is agent eval a thing yet?" | Point to $500M+ in adjacent funding, Gartner/Deloitte reports |
| **"W&B will just build this"** | The "big company risk" objection | Explain why incumbents' DNA is observability, not competition. Different product, different buyer motion |
| **India-based team** | Some US VCs have bias | Target India-friendly VCs (Accel India, Lightspeed India, Peak XV). Or apply to YC (geography-agnostic) |
| **Burn rate concerns** | "How will you spend $3M?" | Show a clear hiring plan + milestone plan |

### The Bottom Line on Funding

> **Funding is gettable.** AI infra is the hottest sector. The positioning is differentiated. The market is validated by $500M+ in adjacent funding. The challenge is not "will VCs be interested?" — it's "can you build enough traction to stand out from the 1000 other AI startups pitching this quarter?"

**The formula: Ship the arena. Publish 3-5 viral benchmark reports. Get 5 design partner LOIs. Then pitch. The raise will come.**

---

## 10. Executive Summary

1. **The market is massive and timing is perfect.** AI agent market: $5B to $47B by 2030 (40%+ CAGR). Agents are going to production NOW. Evaluation tools haven't caught up.

2. **AgentClash occupies an empty quadrant.** No commercial platform does head-to-head agent benchmarking. Chatbot Arena does model chat. LangSmith does call tracing. Nobody does what AgentClash does.

3. **~$500M+ in VC has been deployed into adjacent competitors** (LangSmith, Braintrust, Arize, W&B) — validating the space while leaving the agent-level niche open.

4. **The public arena is the unfair advantage.** No competitor has a public leaderboard + private workspace loop. This is both the GTM engine and the moat. Prioritize arena launch.

5. **W&B is the biggest threat.** $1.25B valuation, 700K users, NVIDIA-backed. If they add agent benchmarking, we need to already own the brand. Move fast.

6. **Year 1 target: $312K ARR (₹2.6Cr). Year 2: $1.4M ARR (₹11.8Cr).** Achievable with 40 Team + 10 Growth + 3 enterprise workspaces by month 12.

7. **Funding is very gettable.** $2-4M seed is realistic. AI infra is the hottest VC category, positioning is differentiated, and comparable companies raised with less.

8. **Model launch days are free marketing events.** When GPT-5 or Claude 5 drops, race it immediately, publish results, own the conversation.

9. **CI/CD integration is the retention lock.** Once teams run AgentClash benchmarks on every PR, switching costs become very high. Build the GitHub Action early.

10. **The replay corpus is the long-term moat.** Millions of agent execution traces become a dataset nobody else has — enabling future products: failure analysis, agent coaching, performance prediction.

---

*Sources: MarketsandMarkets, Grand View Research, Gartner, Forrester, Deloitte, Capgemini, Crunchbase, public funding announcements. Revenue figures for private companies are estimates. Exchange rate: ₹83.5/USD. Market data through early 2025.*

# Quest Strategy — What Communities Actually Want

> Distilled from the March 13 meeting and subsequent brainstorming. The team's central unsolved question: **what is the killer campaign workflow?**

## Central Thesis

Communities say they want "engagement." I suspect that's just vanity metrics — retweets, likes, claim counts. Platforms like Galxe trained them to think in those terms, and now that's the language they use when describing what they need.

What they actually need is **quality growth**. A better, richer experience for community members. Quality contributions. Not more members — better members, and better outcomes from the members they already have.

The existing quest ecosystem is broken. A study of 80 million quest completions ([Quest Love](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.18810v2), Jan 2025) found near-zero retention when rewards stop (-0.18%), bots claiming rewards within 2 minutes of launch, and up to 70% of airdrops going to sybil attackers. Even $0.10 token rewards triggered 12x spikes in completions — but removing them returned activity to baseline. These platforms create the *illusion* of engagement while extracting value.

The hypothesis: if you design quests that are structurally impossible to farm — through encryption, collective conditions, and progressive trust — you get contributors instead of farmers. And one real contributor is worth a hundred airdrop farmers.

There's a deeper problem too. Research on motivation ([Deci et al., 1999](https://home.ubalt.edu/tmitch/642/articles%20syllabus/Deci%20Koestner%20Ryan%20meta%20IM%20psy%20bull%2099.pdf) — meta-analysis of 128 studies) shows that paying people for things they already do voluntarily *reduces* intrinsic motivation. Volunteers who received small payments worked fewer hours than unpaid ones. This means the entire "complete quest, get token" model may be actively counterproductive — turning intrinsically motivated community members into transactional ones.

This needs validating with actual community managers. We can't go to them with abstract claims. We need concrete examples that make them say "yes, that's exactly my problem."

---

## What Communities Are Seeking

> **⚠️ Hypotheses, not facts**
> Based on my experience in Discord communities across: crypto, board games, computer games, music production, hardware, and software development. Needs validating.

### The root need: Core Activity & Adoption

Every community exists around *a thing* — a protocol, a game, a tool, a creative practice. The overarching need is people actively using, building on, or creating with that thing. Without this, the community is hollow.

- **Crypto protocol:** TVL, transaction volume, staking participation, integrations built
- **Game:** Active players, matches played, mods downloaded and used
- **Dev tooling:** Downloads, projects built with it, packages and integrations
- **Creative/hardware:** Creations made and shared, performances, collaborations

All the needs below are in service of this. Knowledgeable contributors explain the thing. Activity organisers create contexts to do the thing. Feedback improves the thing. Onboarding gets new people doing the thing. Trusted operators scale the thing. Sybil resistance protects the thing.

For crypto protocols specifically, this is existential — token price and protocol usage are the metrics that determine survival. For games, it's player count. For dev tools, it's adoption. The community isn't separate from the product — it *is* the growth engine.

### 1. Knowledgeable Contributors

Community members who are as knowledgeable as — if not more than — the core team. Educators, guide writers, modders, wiki editors.

**Why they want it:** These people are force multipliers. One good guide writer saves the team thousands of support interactions. One modder extends the product's lifespan. They're the backbone of any community.

**Why it's hard to obtain:** Knowledge takes time to build and there's no structured pathway from "new member" to "expert contributor." The people who get there do it despite the system, not because of it. There's also no reliable way to reward them — Discord roles are the best most communities have. And per the [motivation crowding research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motivation_crowding_theory), clumsily adding monetary rewards might actually crowd out the intrinsic drive that got them there.

**How you know you've got it:** Community members answering each other's questions accurately. Wiki/docs contributions from non-team members. Mods or guides that the core team didn't build. I got hired at Nucypher partly due to activity in the Brownie discord — this is the dream outcome.

### 2. Activity Organisers & Self-Sustaining Activity

People who create reasons for others to come back — and communities that run themselves. Multiplayer group organisers, tournament runners, event coordinators, jam session hosts. These are two sides of the same coin: activity organisers are the people, self-sustaining activity is the outcome.

**Why they want it:** Admin burnout is real and well-documented. A [study of volunteer moderators](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/14614448221138529) found the number 1 reason mods quit is interpersonal conflict within mod teams, followed by time constraints. [Discord's own 2025 survey](https://discord.com/safety/understanding-and-avoiding-moderator-burnout) of 500+ moderators acknowledged burnout as a systemic problem. If the community only lives when the admin is actively pushing content, it dies the moment they take a holiday.

**Why it's hard to obtain:** It requires initiative and social capital that can't be manufactured. You can't quest someone into being an organiser — but you can recognise and reward the ones who emerge naturally. Most communities have no mechanism for this beyond "give them a Discord role."

**How you know you've got it:** Events happening that the core team didn't initiate. Regular recurring activities with consistent attendance. The Discord is active when the core team is offline. Members onboard other members.

### 3. Quality Feedback

Bug reporters, balance testers, governance participants who actually read proposals. High-signal feedback as opposed to noise.

**Why they want it:** Any community with an evolving product — game, protocol, hardware — needs to know what's broken and what's working. But most feedback channels are either silent or full of low-effort complaints.

**Why it's hard to obtain:** Quality feedback requires understanding the product well enough to articulate what's wrong (see 1.). It also requires effort with no immediate payoff — writing a detailed bug report takes 30 minutes for something the team might already know about.

**How you know you've got it:** Bug reports that include reproduction steps. Governance proposals that reference prior discussions. Feature requests that account for technical constraints. Feedback that changes what the team builds.

### 4. Onboarding That Converts

Turning lurkers into participants. The lurker-to-participant gap is massive — most members join and never say a word (I'm normally one of those).

**Why they want it:** Every community is a funnel. [Nielsen's 90-9-1 rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/) (well-replicated) says 90% lurk, 9% contribute occasionally, 1% create most content. [More recent data](https://www.higherlogic.com/blog/90-9-1-rule-online-community-engagement-data/) suggests ~20% participate in medium-to-large communities, but that still means 80% are silent. Widening any stage of that funnel has compounding effects.

**Why it's hard to obtain:** The first action is the hardest. New members don't know what's expected, don't know the norms, and are afraid of looking stupid. Most onboarding is a pinned message that nobody reads. A [2025 Reddit field experiment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12693982/) found that positive feedback on first posts and first-timer-specific prompts were the most effective conversion interventions — but most communities don't do either systematically.

**How you know you've got it:** New members posting within their first week. A visible pathway from "just joined" to "first contribution." Decreasing ratio of lurkers to participants over time. Key insight from the research: [84% of members exhibit mixed behaviour](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0747563214003008) — they lurk in some communities and participate in others. It's situational, not a permanent identity. The right structure can convert them.

### 5. Trusted Operators

Knowing who you can delegate responsibility to. Mod powers, treasury management, tournament admin, grant review.

**Why they want it:** Scaling a community means delegating, and delegating means trust. In crypto: who gets multisig keys? Who reviews grant applications? In gaming: who runs the tournament? Who curates the mod repository?

**Why it's hard to obtain:** Outside crypto, it's pure vibes-based trust — "this person seems reliable, give them mod." No audit trail, no revocation logic, no shared accountability. Crypto at least has multisigs and on-chain history, but it's still mostly informal. There's no portable, verifiable reputation system.

**How you know you've got it:** You can go on holiday without worrying. Delegated tasks get done to the same standard. Community members trust the operators, not just the core team.

### 6. Sybil Resistance

Keeping bots and bad actors out without making the front door annoying for real people.

**Why they want it:** Every community with any value — airdrops, rewards, early access, competitive rankings — gets farmed. The farmers extract value and degrade the experience for real members. The [Quest Love study](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.18810v2) found reward depletion times dropping from 12 hours to under 30 minutes as bot automation improved.

**Why it's hard to obtain:** Current tools are blunt instruments — captchas, phone verification, minimum account age. They stop the laziest bots but not determined farmers. And every additional gate reduces legitimate sign-ups too. The fundamental problem is that most quests are designed to be *easy to complete* — which means they're easy to automate.

**How you know you've got it:** Reward recipients are real people who stick around after the reward. No sudden spikes of identical wallets. Quest completion requires human judgement or collaboration that can't be scripted.

---

## Discord Server Archetypes

Based on communities I'm part of. Limited sample but spans a useful range.

### Crypto / Protocol Communities
**Examples:** Ethereum, Brownie/Ape, Threshold, Collabland communities, TACo

- Largest overlap with all 6 needs — treasury governance, contributor pipelines, sybil resistance all critical
- Most likely to have on-chain components already (token-gated channels, governance votes)
- Strongest airdrop farming problem — every incentive gets gamed
- Community manager is often a dedicated role or even a team
- **Dominant needs:** sybil resistance, knowledgeable contributors, trusted operators

### Developer Tooling
**Examples:** Brownie/Ape, Python, TACo

- Quality feedback is literally the product — bug reports, feature requests, and PRs are the lifeblood
- Knowledgeable contributors write the docs, answer questions, build integrations
- A big draw for members: seeing new things people have built, learning new techniques, and job opportunities
- Less concerned with sybil resistance (nothing to farm) but very concerned with onboarding — getting new devs from "installed it" to "built something"
- Often maintained by a tiny team or a single person — admin burnout is acute
- **Dominant needs:** quality feedback, knowledgeable contributors, onboarding that converts

### Strategy / Board Games
**Examples:** Baduk (Go) servers, Civ7, One More Turn, Ursa Ryan

- Strategy discussion is the lifeblood — probably the most active channels in these servers
- Activity organisers run regular multiplayer sessions, tournaments, teaching games
- Mod ecosystem (Civ) creates knowledgeable contributors who extend the game's life
- Self-sustaining activity is the norm in healthy gaming communities — they don't need the dev team
- Sybil resistance matters for competitive contexts (tournaments, rankings) but less so for casual play
- **Dominant needs:** activity organisers, knowledgeable contributors (strategy/teaching), quality feedback (balance/mods)

### Creative / Hardware Niche
**Examples:** Dirtywave M8, mylarmelodies

- Tight-knit, passionate communities around specific hardware or creative practice
- Lots of sharing creations — patches, tracks, sample packs, techniques. Show-and-tell is a core activity
- Activity organisers run jam sessions, collaborative projects, tutorial series
- Knowledgeable contributors write the unofficial guides the manufacturer never made
- Very low sybil risk (nothing to farm), very high onboarding need (hardware has a learning curve)
- **Dominant needs:** activity organisers, knowledgeable contributors, onboarding that converts

### Similarities Across All Types

- **Lurker-to-participant gap is universal.** 80%+ silent members regardless of domain.
- **Admin burnout scales with community size.** The bigger the community, the more this matters.
- **The best contributors are intrinsically motivated.** People get involved because they WANT to. Quest design must amplify intrinsic motivation, not replace it with extrinsic rewards that crowd it out.
- **Trust and delegation** are universal problems. Every community needs to know who they can rely on.
- **Showing and discussing work** is a core activity everywhere — crypto projects share builds, devs share tools, gamers share strategies, musicians share patches.

### Key Differences

- **Sybil resistance** is primarily a crypto problem (where there's money to extract). Gaming/creative communities rarely face it at scale.
- **Treasury/governance** is mostly crypto-specific today. Non-crypto shared funds are rare — mainly OSS (Open Collective), in-game currencies (WoW guild banks), and Patreon-funded communities. But these are almost always single-admin-controlled, not collectively governed.
- **On-chain actions** are natural in crypto, foreign everywhere else. Non-crypto quest archetypes must work without requiring users to understand blockchain.

---

## TACo Value Propositions

From Arjun's outline in the March 13 meeting:

### Cheaper
Existing campaign platforms are expensive — Galxe, Zealy, Layer3 charge significant fees. Opportunity to target the **long tail of mid-sized projects** not spending millions on campaigns. Lower barrier = more experimentation from community managers.

### Discord-Native (No Context Switching)
Campaigns happen where the community already lives. No "click this link, go to an external platform, connect wallet, come back." The entire flow stays in Discord. This matters because every redirect loses participants.

### Mercenary Avoidance
Discord campaigns reach community members who are already there — not random Galxe farmers browsing a leaderboard. If you're already in a DAO's Discord, you've passed a filter. The quest design can then further filter for quality within that base.

### Auditable Flows
On-chain verification that someone actually did the thing. Provable completion, not self-reported. Timing data reveals bots (2-second completions vs 20-minute genuine engagement).

### Guardrails for Novices
Programmable conditions abstract away complexity. A novice doesn't need to understand LPs, contract addresses, or gas — they see a button, a confirmation, and a result. The conditions ensure they can't accidentally do something catastrophic.

### Collective Oversight
The unique structural advantage no other wallet has — multiple people with differing incentives governing shared resources. Hierarchical oversight, not just multisig. This maps directly to trusted operators.

### Cross-Server Portable Identity
Reputation that follows you across communities. Expensive to sybil across multiple servers with one identity. If you're a quality contributor in community A, community B can see that. This doesn't exist today.

---

## Quest Archetypes — TACo-Native

> **⚠️ Hypotheses** — These need testing with actual community managers. The question for each: does this solve a problem you actually have?

The key design principle: **quests should be things that are impossible or impractical without TACo.** If Galxe or Zealy could do it, it's not differentiated. TACo uniquely enables encryption-gated content, collective conditions, progressive on-chain trust, and cross-server reputation. The archetypes below lean into these.

Second principle: **amplify intrinsic motivation, don't replace it.** The [research is clear](https://home.ubalt.edu/tmitch/642/articles%20syllabus/Deci%20Koestner%20Ryan%20meta%20IM%20psy%20bull%2099.pdf) that monetary rewards for voluntary contributions can backfire. The best quests create *structures* that make intrinsically motivated people more effective, and use conditions to filter out mercenaries — rather than trying to bribe mercenaries into becoming contributors.

### 1. Collective Unlock — Encrypted Content That Requires Group Effort

A piece of valuable content — alpha, research, strategy, early access, dlc — is encrypted via TACo. It only decrypts when a group of participants has collectively met a set of conditions.

**How it works:**
- Community admin encrypts content (e.g., exclusive strategy guide, early feature access, alpha research, premium content)
- Decryption condition: N members must each independently complete a prerequisite (e.g., complete a tutorial, submit feedback, participate in a discussion)
- Nobody can access the content until enough people have genuinely contributed
- No single person can farm this — it requires real, distributed human participation

**Why it's new:** This is structurally impossible on Galxe/Zealy. Encryption-gated collective conditions don't exist anywhere else. It creates genuine cooperation rather than parallel farming.

**Satisfies:** knowledgeable contributors, onboarding that converts, sybil resistance
**TACo props:** collective oversight, auditable flows, guardrails
**Works for:** crypto (alpha/research access), gaming (early access to new content/mods), dev tooling (beta features), creative (exclusive sample packs or tutorials from well-known creators)

### 2. Progressive Trust Ladder — Earn Real Capabilities, Not Just Roles

A quest chain where completing stages grants escalating *on-chain capabilities*, not just Discord roles. Trust is earned through demonstrated behaviour and automatically revocable if violated.

**How it works:**
- **Stage 1:** Complete onboarding → can execute pre-approved transactions (e.g., claim rewards, vote on simple proposals)
- **Stage 2:** Sustained activity over N weeks → can propose transactions for community review
- **Stage 3:** Track record of good proposals → can approve others' transactions within limits
- **Stage 4:** Long-term trusted operator → elevated spending authority with collective oversight guardrails
- At every stage, conditions define what you can and can't do. Violation or inactivity automatically downgrades capabilities.

**Why it's new:** Discord roles are binary and trust-based. This is a continuous, on-chain, condition-enforced trust gradient with automatic revocation. No platform does this. It's what "trusted operators" looks like when you have programmable conditions.

**Satisfies:** trusted operators, onboarding that converts, knowledgeable contributors (the ladder incentivises learning)
**TACo props:** collective oversight, guardrails, cross-server portable identity, auditable flows
**Works for:** crypto DAOs (governance progression), gaming (tournament admin privileges), any community that needs to delegate safely

### 3. Blind Submission + Reveal — Encrypted Peer Review

Participants submit work encrypted. Submissions only decrypt after a deadline — preventing copying and enabling genuine blind review.

**How it works:**
- Quest: create something (strategy guide, mod, art, code contribution, governance proposal)
- Submit via TACo encryption with time-based decryption condition (unlocks at deadline)
- After deadline: all submissions decrypt simultaneously
- Community peer review on decrypted content (with tenure-gated voting to prevent sybil manipulation)
- Rewards based on peer assessment, not self-reporting

**Why it's new:** Time-locked encryption for submissions is something only TACo can provide in a decentralised way. It solves the copying problem that plagues every content creation quest, and creates genuine creative/intellectual competition.

**Satisfies:** knowledgeable contributors, quality feedback (the review process itself)
**TACo props:** auditable flows, mercenary avoidance (tenure-gated review), Discord-native
**Works for:** gaming (strategy contests, mod competitions), creative (remix challenges, jam sessions with blind submissions), dev tooling (hackathon-style sprints), crypto (governance proposal competitions)

### 4. Meritocratic Treasury — Earn Spending Authority

Community members earn increasing authority to spend from a shared treasury, with guardrails that automatically tighten or loosen based on track record. Not just multisig — *conditional delegation*.

**How it works:**
- Community treasury exists with collective oversight conditions
- New members: can request grants up to $X, requires M-of-N approval
- Established members: can spend up to $Y without approval for pre-approved categories (bounties, event prizes, etc.)
- Track record determines limits — successful grants that produce results → higher authority. Failed or disputed grants → reduced authority.
- All fully auditable, all condition-enforced, all automatically revocable.

**Why it's new:** Multisigs are all-or-nothing (you're a signer or you're not). This is graduated, conditional, and reputation-linked. It's what DAOs have always wanted but couldn't build — and it extends to non-crypto communities that manage any shared resources.

**Satisfies:** trusted operators, activity organisers (they get budgets for events), self-sustaining activity
**TACo props:** collective oversight (the entire point), guardrails, auditable flows, cross-server portable identity
**Works for:** crypto DAOs (grant committees, bounty funds), gaming (tournament prize pools), OSS (bounty management), any community with shared resources — even Patreon-funded ones

### 5. Reputation Staking — Vouch With Skin in the Game

Members can vouch for others by staking their own cross-server reputation. Creates accountability networks that make trust portable.

**How it works:**
- Established member vouches for a newcomer
- Voucher's reputation score is partially at risk
- If the newcomer performs well (completes quests, earns positive peer review), both benefit
- If the newcomer acts badly (sybil behaviour, bad-faith participation), voucher's score decreases
- Reputation is cross-server portable — vouching in one community affects your standing everywhere

**Why it's new:** No platform ties personal reputation to vouching in a verifiable, cross-server way. This creates genuine social accountability — the kind that already exists informally in tight-knit communities, but made portable and auditable.

**Satisfies:** sybil resistance, onboarding that converts (social onboarding via trusted members), trusted operators
**TACo props:** cross-server portable identity, auditable flows, conditions
**Works for:** crypto (anti-sybil for airdrops/governance), gaming (tournament integrity), any community where knowing who vouches for whom matters

---

## How Archetypes Map to Communities

| Archetype | Crypto/DAO | Dev Tooling | Gaming/Strategy | Creative |
|-----------|:----------:|:-----------:|:---------------:|:--------:|
| Collective Unlock | alpha/research | beta features | early content access | exclusive tutorials |
| Trust Ladder | governance progression | maintainer path | tournament admin | curator roles |
| Blind Submission | proposal contests | hackathons | strategy competitions | remix challenges |
| Meritocratic Treasury | grant committees | bounty funds | tournament prizes | shared project budgets |
| Reputation Staking | anti-sybil | contributor vouching | competitive integrity | — |
title: Quest Strategy — What Communities Actually Want

body:
How to Rank 10% in Your First Kaggle Competition

http://bit.ly/2FH8Pw3

About 0 Minutes

Introduction

Kaggle is the best place to learn from other data scientists. Many companies provide data and prize money to set up data science competitions on Kaggle. Recently I had my first shot on Kaggle and ranked 98th (~ 5%) among 2125 teams. Being my Kaggle debut, I feel quite satisfied with the result. Since many Kaggle beginners set 10% as their first goal, I want to share my two cents on how to achieve that.

This post is also available in Chinese.

Updated on Oct 28th, 2016: I made many wording changes and added several updates to this post. Note that Kaggle has went through some major changes since I published this post, especially with its ranking system. Therefore some descriptions here might not apply anymore.

Most Kagglers use Python or R. I prefer Python, but R users should have no difficulty in understanding the ideas behind tools and languages.

First let’s go through some facts about Kaggle competitions in case you are not familiar with them.

  • Different competitions have different tasks: classifications, regressions, recommendations… Training set and testing set will be open for download after the competition launches.

  • A competition typically lasts for 2 ~ 3 months. Each team can submit for a limited number of times per day. Usually it’s 5 times a day.

  • There will be a 1st submission deadline one week before the end of the competition, after which you cannot merge teams or enter the competition. Therefore be sure to have at least one valid submission before that.

  • You will get you score immediately after the submission. Different competitions use different scoring metrics, which are explained by the question mark on the leaderboard.

  • The score you get is calculated on a subset of testing set, which is commonly referred to as a Public LB score. Whereas the final result will use the remaining data in the testing set, which is referred to as a Private LB score.

  • The score you get by local cross validation is commonly referred to as a CV score. Generally speaking, CV scores are more reliable than LB scores.

  • Beginners can learn a lot from Forum and Scripts. Do not hesitate to ask about anything. Kagglers are in general very kind and helpful.

I assume that readers are familiar with basic concepts and models of machine learning. Enjoy reading!

General Approach

In this section, I will walk you through the process of a Kaggle competition.

Data Exploration

What we do at this stage is called EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis), which means analytically exploring data in order to provide some insights for subsequent processing and modeling.

Usually we would load the data using Pandas and make some visualizations to understand the data.

Visualization

For plotting, Matplotlib and Seaborn should suffice.

Some common practices:

  • Inspect the distribution of target variable. Depending on what scoring metric is used, an imbalanced distribution of target variable might harm the model’s performance.
  • For numerical variables, use box plot and scatter plot to inspect their distributions and check for outliers.
  • For classification tasks, plot the data with points colored according to their labels. This can help with feature engineering.
  • Make pairwise distribution plots and examine their correlations.

Be sure to read this inspiring tutorial of exploratory visualization before you go on.

Statistical Tests

We can perform some statistical tests to confirm our hypotheses. Sometimes we can get enough intuition from visualization, but quantitative results are always good to have. Note that we will always encounter non-i.i.d. data in real world. So we have to be careful about which test to use and how we interpret the findings.

In many competitions public LB scores are not very consistent with local CV scores due to noise or non-i.i.d. distribution. You can use test results to roughly set a threshold for determining whether an increase of score is due to genuine improvment or randomness.

Data Preprocessing

In most cases, we need to preprocess the dataset before constructing features. Some common steps are:

  • Sometimes several files are provided and we need to join them.
  • Deal with missing data.
  • Deal with outliers.
  • Encode categorical variables if necessary.
  • Deal with noise. For example you may have some floats derived from raw figures. The loss of precision during floating-point arithemics can bring much noise into the data: two seemingly different values might be the same before conversion. Sometimes noise harms model and we would want to avoid that.

How we choose to perform preprocessing largely depends on what we learn about the data in the previous stage. In practice, I recommend using Jupyter Notebook for data manipulation and mastering usage of frequently used Pandas operations. The advantage is that you get to see the results immediately and are able to modify or rerun code blocks. This also makes it very convenient to share your approach with others. After all reproducible results are very important in data science.

Let’s see some examples.

Outlier

The plot shows some scaled coordinates data. We can see that there are some outliers in the top-right corner. Exclude them and the distribution looks good.

Dummy Variables

For categorical variables, a common practice is One-hot Encoding. For a categorical variable with n possible values, we create a group of n dummy variables. Suppose a record in the data takes one value for this variable, then the corresponding dummy variable is set to 1 while other dummies in the same group are all set to 0.

In this example, we transform DayOfWeek into 7 dummy variables.

Note that when the categorical variable can take many values (hundreds or more), this might not work well. It’s difficult to find a general solution to that, but I’ll discuss one scenario in the next section.

Feature Engineering

Some describe the essence of Kaggle competitions as feature engineering supplemented by model tuning and ensemble learning. Yes, that makes a lot of sense. Feature engineering gets your very far. Yet it is how well you know about the domain of given data that decides how far you can go. For example, in a competition where data is mainly consisted of texts, Natural Language Processing teachniques are a must. The approach of constructing useful features is something we all have to continuously learn in order to do better.

Basically, when you feel that a variable is intuitively useful for the task, you can include it as a feature. But how do you know it actually works? The simplest way is to plot it against the target variable like this:

Feature Selection

Generally speaking, we should try to craft as many features as we can and have faith in the model’s ability to pick up the most significant features. Yet there’s still something to gain from feature selection beforehand:

  • Less features mean faster training
  • Some features are linearly related to others. This might put a strain on the model.
  • By picking up the most important features, we can use interactions between them as new features. Sometimes this gives surprising improvement.

The simplest way to inspect feature importance is by fitting a random forest model. There are more robust feature selection algorithms (e.g. this) which are theoretically superior but not practicable due to the absence of efficient implementation. You can combat noisy data (to an extent) simply by increasing number of trees used in a random forest.

This is important for competitions in which data is anonymized because you won’t waste time trying to figure out the meaning of a variable that’s of no significance.

Feature Encoding

Sometimes raw features have to be converted to some other formats for them to work properly.

For example, suppose we have a categorical variable which can take more than 10K different values. Then naively creating dummy variables is not a feasible option. An acceptable solution is to create dummy variables for only a subset of the values (e.g. values that constitute 95% of the feature importance) and assign everything else to an ‘others’ class.

Updated on Oct 28th, 2016: For the scenario described above, another possible solution is to use Factorized Machines. Please refer to this post by Kaggle user “idle_speculation” for details.

Model Selection

When the features are set, we can start training models. Kaggle competitions usually favor tree-based models:

  • Gradient Boosted Trees
  • Random Forest
  • Extra Randomized Trees

The following models are slightly worse in terms of general performance, but are suitable as base models in ensemble learning (will be discussed later):

  • SVM
  • Linear Regression
  • Logistic Regression
  • Neural Networks

Note that this does not apply to computer vision competitions which are pretty much dominated by neural network models.

All these models are implemented in Sklearn.

Here I want to emphasize the greatness of Xgboost. The outstanding performance of gradient boosted trees and Xgboost’s efficient implementation makes it very popular in Kaggle competitions. Nowadays almost every winner uses Xgboost in one way or another.

Updated on Oct 28th, 2016: Recently Microsoft open sourced LightGBM, a potentially better library than Xgboost for gradient boosting.

By the way, for Windows users installing Xgboost could be a painstaking process. You can refer to this post by me if you run into problems.

Model Training

We can improve a model’s performance by tuning its parameters. A model usually have many parameters, but only a few of them are significant to its performance. For example, the most important parameters for a random forset is the number of trees in the forest and the maximum number of features used in developing each tree. We need to understand how models work and what impact does each parameter have to the model’s performance, be it accuracy, robustness or speed.

Normally we would find the best set of parameters by a process called grid search. Actually what it does is simply iterating through all the possible combinations and find the best one.

By the way, random forest usually reach optimum when max_features is set to the square root of the total number of features.

Here I’d like to stress some points about tuning XGB. These parameters are generally considered to have real impacts on its performance:

  • eta: Step size used in updating weights. Lower eta means slower training but better convergence.
  • num_round: Total number of iterations.
  • subsample: The ratio of training data used in each iteration. This is to combat overfitting.
  • colsample_bytree: The ratio of features used in each iteration. This is like max_features in RandomForestClassifier.
  • max_depth: The maximum depth of each tree. Unlike random forest, gradient boosting would eventually overfit if we do not limit its depth.
  • early_stopping_rounds: If we don’t see an increase of validation score for a given number of iterations, the algorithm will stop early. This is to combat overfitting, too.

Usual tuning steps:

  1. Reserve a portion of training set as the validation set.
  2. Set eta to a relatively high value (e.g. 0.05 ~ 0.1), num_round to 300 ~ 500.
  3. Use grid search to find the best combination of other parameters.
  4. Gradually lower eta until we reach the optimum.
  5. Use the validation set as watch_list to re-train the model with the best parameters. Observe how score changes on validation set in each iteration. Find the optimal value for early_stopping_rounds.

Finally, note that models with randomness all have a parameter like seed or random_state to control the random seed. You must record this with all other parameters when you get a good model. Otherwise you wouldn’t be able to reproduce it.

Cross Validation

Cross validation is an essential step in model training. It tells us whether our model is at high risk of overfitting. In many competitions, public LB scores are not very reliable. Often when we improve the model and get a better local CV score, the LB score becomes worse. It is widely believed that we should trust our CV scores under such situation. Ideally we would want CV scores obtained by different approaches to improve in sync with each other and with the LB score, but this is not always possible.

Usually 5-fold CV is good enough. If we use more folds, the CV score would become more reliable, but the training takes longer to finish as well. However, we shouldn’t use too many folds if our training data is limited. Otherwise we would have too few samples in each fold to guarantee statistical significance.

How to do CV properly is not a trivial problem. It requires constant experiment and case-by-case discussion. Many Kagglers share their CV approaches (like this one) after competitions when they feel that reliable CV is not easy.

Ensemble Generation

Ensemble Learning refers to the technique of combining different models. It reduces both bias and variance of the final model (you can find a proof here), thus increasing the score and reducing the risk of overfitting. Recently it became virtually impossible to win prize without using ensemble in Kaggle competitions.

Common approaches of ensemble learning are:

  • Bagging: Use different random subsets of training data to train each base model. Then all the base models vote to generate the final predictions. This is how random forest works.

  • Boosting: Train base models iteratively, modify the weights of training samples according to the last iteration. This is how gradient boosted trees work. (Actually it’s not the whole story. Apart from boosting, GBTs try to learn the residuals of earlier iterations.) It performs better than bagging but is more prone to overfitting.

  • Blending: Use non-overlapping data to train different base models and take a weighted average of them to obtain the final predictions. This is easy to implement but uses less data.

  • Stacking: To be discussed next.

In theory, for the ensemble to perform well, two factors matter:

  • Base models should be as unrelated as possibly. This is why we tend to include non-tree-based models in the ensemble even though they don’t perform as well. The math says that the greater the diversity, and less bias in the final ensemble.
  • Performance of base models shouldn’t differ to much.

Actually we have a trade-off here. In practice we may end up with highly related models of comparable performances. Yet we ensemble them anyway because it usually increase the overall performance.

Stacking

Compared with blending, stacking makes better use of training data. Here’s a diagram of how it works:

(Taken from Faron. Many thanks!)

It’s much like cross validation. Take 5-fold stacking as an example. First we split the training data into 5 folds. Next we will do 5 iterations. In each iteration, train every base model on 4 folds and predict on the hold-out fold. You have to keep the predictions on the testing data as well. This way, in each iteration every base model will make predictions on 1 fold of the training data and all of the testing data. After 5 iterations we will obtain a matrix of shape #(samples in training data) X #(base models). This matrix is then fed to the stacker (it’s just another model) in the second level. After the stacker is fitted, use the predictions on testing data by base models (each base model is trained 5 times, therefore we have to take an average to obtain a matrix of the same shape) as the input for the stacker and obtain our final predictions.

Maybe it’s better to just show the codes:

Prize winners usually have larger and much more complicated ensembles. For beginner, implementing a correct 5-fold stacking is good enough.

*Pipeline

We can see that the workflow for a Kaggle competition is quite complex, especially for model selection and ensemble. Ideally, we need a highly automated pipeline capable of:

  • Modularized feature transformations. We only need to write a few lines of codes (or better, rules / DSLs) and the new feature is added to the training set.
  • Automated grid search. We only need to set up models and parameter grid, the search will be run and the best parameters will be recorded.
  • Automated ensemble selection. Use K best models for training the ensemble as soon as we put another base model into the pool.

For beginners, the first one is not very important because the number of features is quite manageable; the third one is not important either because typically we only do several ensembles at the end of the competition. But the second one is good to have because manually recording the performance and parameters of each model is time-consuming and error-prone.

Chenglong Chen, the winner of Crowdflower Search Results Relevance, once released his pipeline on GitHub. It’s very complete and efficient. Yet it’s very hard to understand and extract all his logic to build a general framework. This is something you might want to do when you have plenty of time.

Home Depot Search Relevance

In this section I will share my solution in Home Depot Search Relevance Competition and what I learned from top teams after the competition.

The task in this competition is to predict how relevant a result is for a search term on Home Depot website. The relevance is an average score from three human evaluators and ranges between 1 ~ 3. Therefore it’s a regression task. The datasets contains search terms, product titles / descriptions and some attributes like brand, size and color. The metric is RMSE.

This is much like Crowdflower Search Results Relevance. The difference is that Quadratic Weighted Kappa is used in Crowdflower competition and therefore complicated the final cutoff of regression scores. Also there were no attributes provided in Crowdflower.

EDA

There were several quite good EDAs by the time I joined the competition, especially this one. I learned that:

  • Many search terms / products appeared several times.
  • Text similarities are great features.
  • Many products don’t have attributes features. Would this be a problem?
  • Product ID seems to have strong predictive power. However the overlap of product ID between the training set and the testing set is not very high. Would this contribute to overfitting?

Preprocessing

You can find how I did preprocessing and feature engineering on GitHub. I’ll only give a brief summary here:

  1. Use typo dictionary posted in the forum to correct typos in search terms.
  2. Count attributes. Find those frequent and easily exploited ones.
  3. Join the training set with the testing set. This is important because otherwise you’ll have to do feature transformation twice.
  4. Do stemming and tokenizing for all the text fields. Some normalization (with digits and units) and synonym substitutions are performed manually.

Feature

  • *Attribute Features
    • Whether the product contains a certain attribute (brand, size, color, weight, indoor/outdoor, energy star certified …)
    • Whether a certain attribute matches with the search term

  • Meta Features

    • Length of each text field
    • Whether the product contains attribute fields
    • Brand (encoded as integers)
    • Product ID

  • Matching

    • Whether search term appears in product title / description / attributes
    • Count and ratio of search term’s appearance in product title / description / attributes
    • *Whether the i-th word of search term appears in product title / description / attributes

  • Text similarities between search term and product title/description/attributes

  • Latent Semantic Indexing: By performing SVD decomposition to the matrix obtained from BOW/TF-IDF Vectorization, we get a latent representation of different search term / product groups. This enables our model to distinguish between groups and assign different weights to features, therefore solving the issue of dependent data and products lacking some features (to an extent).

Note that features listed above with * are the last batch of features I added. The problem is that the model trained on data that included these features performed worse than the previous ones. At first I thought that the increase in number of features would require re-tuning of model parameters. However, after wasting much CPU time on grid search, I still could not beat the old model. I think it might be the issue of feature correlation mentioned above. I actually knew a solution that might work, which is to combine models trained on different version of features by stacking. Unfortunately I didn’t have enough time to try it. As a matter of fact, most of top teams regard the ensemble of models trained with different preprocessing and feature engineering pipelines as a key to success.

Model

At first I was using RandomForestRegressor to build my model. Then I tried Xgboost and it turned out to be more than twice as fast as Sklearn. From that on what I do everyday is basically running grid search on my work station while working on features on my laptop.

Dataset in this competition is not trivial to validate. It’s not i.i.d. and many records are dependent. Many times I used better features / parameters only to end with worse LB scores. As repeatedly stated by many accomplished Kagglers, you have to trust your own CV score under such situation. Therefore I decided to use 10-fold instead of 5-fold in cross validation and ignore the LB score in the following attempts.

Ensemble

My final model is an ensemble consisting of 4 base models:

  • RandomForestRegressor
  • ExtraTreesRegressor
  • GradientBoostingRegressor
  • XGBRegressor

The stacker is also a XGBRegressor.

The problem is that all my base models are highly correlated (with a lowest correlation of 0.9). I thought of including linear regression, SVM regression and XGBRegressor with linear booster into the ensemble, but these models had RMSE scores that are 0.02 higher (this accounts for a gap of hundreds of places on the leaderboard) than the 4 models I finally used. Therefore I decided not to use more models although they would have brought much more diversity.

The good news is that, despite base models being highly correlated, stacking still bumps up my score a lot. What’s more, my CV score and LB score are in complete sync after I started stacking.

During the last two days of the competition, I did one more thing: use 20 or so different random seeds to generate the ensemble and take a weighted average of them as the final submission. This is actually a kind of bagging. It makes sense in theory because in stacking I used 80% of the data to train base models in each iteration, whereas 100% of the data is used to train the stacker. Therefore it’s less clean. Making multiple runs with different seeds makes sure that different 80% of the data are used each time, thus reducing the risk of information leak. Yet by doing this I only achieved an increase of 0.0004, which might be just due to randomness.

After the competition, I found out that my best single model scores 0.46378 on the private leaderboard, whereas my best stacking ensemble scores 0.45849. That was the difference between the 174th place and the 98th place. In other words, feature engineering and model tuning got me into 10%, whereas stacking got me into 5%.

Lessons Learned

There’s much to learn from the solutions shared by top teams:

  • There’s a pattern in the product title. For example, whether a product is accompanied by a certain accessory will be indicated by With/Without XXX at the end of the title.

  • Use external data. For example use WordNet or Reddit Comments Dataset to train synonyms and hypernyms.

  • Some features based on letters instead of words. At first I was rather confused by this. But it makes perfect sense if you consider it. For example, the team that won the 3rd place took the number of letters matched into consideration when computing text similarity. They argued that longer words are more specific and thus more likely to be assigned high relevance scores by human. They also used char-by-char sequence comparison (difflib.SequenceMatcher) to measure visual similarity, which they claimed to be important for human.

  • POS-tag words and find head in phrases and use them when computing various distance metrics.

  • Extract top-ranking trigrams from the TF-IDF of product title / description field and compute the ratio of word from search terms that appear in these trigrams. Vice versa. This is like computing latent indexes from another point of view.

  • Some novel distance metrics like Word Movers Distance

  • Apart from SVD, some used NMF.

  • Generate pairwise polynomial interactions between top-ranking features.

  • For CV, construct splits in which product IDs do not overlap between training set and testing set, and splits in which IDs do. Then we can use these with corresponding ratio to approximate the impact of public/private LB split in our local CV.

Summary

Takeaways

  1. It was a good call to start doing ensembles early in the competition. As it turned out, I was still playing with features during the very last days.
  2. It’s of high priority that I build a pipeline capable of automatic model training and recording best parameters.
  3. Features matter the most! I didn’t spend enough time on features in this competition.
  4. If possible, spend some time to manually inspect raw data for patterns.

Issues Raised

Several issues I encountered in this competitions are of high research values.

  1. How to do reliable CV with dependent data.
  2. How to quantify the trade-off between diversity and accuracy in ensemble learning.
  3. How to deal with feature interaction which harms the model’s performance. And how to determine whether new features are effective in such situations.

Beginner Tips

  1. Choose a competition you’re interested in. It would be better if you’ve already have some insights about the problem domain.
  2. Following my approach or somebody else’s, start exploring, understanding and modeling data.
  3. Learn from forum and scripts. See how others interpret data and construct features.
  4. Find winner interviews / blog posts of previous competitions. They’re extremely helpful, especially if from competitions that share some similarities with that one you’re working on.
  5. Start doing ensemble after you have reached a pretty good score (e.g. 10% ~ 20%) or you feel that there isn’t much room for new features (which, sadly, always turns out to be false).
  6. If you think you may have a chance to win the prize, try teaming up!
  7. Don’t give up until the end of the competition. At least try something new every day.
  8. Learn from the sharings of top teams after the competition. Reflect on your approaches. If possible, spend some time verifying what you learn.
  9. Get some rest!

Reference

  1. Beating Kaggle the Easy Way - Dong Ying
  2. Search Results Relevance Winner’s Interview: 1st place, Chenglong Chen
  3. (Chinese) Solution for Prudential Life Insurance Assessment - Nutastray
